title: Conflict Management
tagline: Turn clashes into progress: diagnose disagreements, choose the right response, negotiate on interests and mediate your team back to work.
description:
Every workplace has disagreements. The question is whether they sharpen decisions or poison teams. This certification gives team leaders, managers and professionals a practical toolkit for the moment a disagreement turns into a conflict: at the plant, on the sales floor, in the boardroom or on a heated WhatsApp group.

You will learn to **diagnose** a conflict by its source (task, process, relationship or values) and by how far it has escalated, to **choose** deliberately between competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating, to **regulate** your own emotions and de-escalate others, and to hold the difficult conversation you have been putting off.

Then you move to the harder tools: **interest-based negotiation** (positions versus interests, BATNA, walk-away points and the zone of possible agreement), a step-by-step **mediation** method for managers, cross-department and family-business conflict, face-saving and hierarchy in Pakistani workplaces, disputes with customers and vendors, prevention through clear roles and agreements, and knowing exactly when a matter must leave your desk and go to HR or a formal process.

Five stages, a ten-question test after each, and a tough timed final exam built from realistic Pakistani workplace scenarios.
audience: Team leaders and supervisors who have to sort out disagreements inside their teams
Middle and senior managers handling friction between departments, regions or functions
HR business partners and people managers who mediate and advise on grievances
Professionals who negotiate with customers, distributors and vendors
Family members and professional managers working together in family-owned businesses
outcomes: Diagnose a workplace conflict by its source and its stage of escalation, and judge how urgently to act
Choose and justify the most suitable conflict-handling mode for a situation, including your own default
Regulate your own emotions, de-escalate a heated person and structure a difficult conversation
Negotiate on interests rather than positions using BATNA, walk-away points and the zone of possible agreement
Mediate a dispute between two team members or departments using a clear step-by-step process
Handle conflict sensitively in Pakistani workplaces, including hierarchy, face-saving and family-business dynamics
Prevent conflict through clear roles and agreements, and know when to escalate to HR or a formal grievance

quest.name: The Eid Season Truce
quest.premise: You have just been promoted to Commercial Operations Lead at Noor Mithaas Foods, a family-owned sweets and snacks maker with a plant in Lahore and a sales hub in Karachi. Six weeks before Eid, a failed corporate gift-box order has the plant and the sales team at war, a key distributor is threatening to walk and the founding family is split over a new product line. With mentor Farhana Qureshi, master five stages of conflict management, then face the final boss: the Eid Summit, where the truce must hold.

badge.name: Common Ground Builder
badge.description: Awarded to professionals who can diagnose a conflict, calm it, negotiate on interests and mediate people back to working together.

cast.name: Farhana Qureshi
cast.role: Head of People and Culture, your mentor

sessions.title: What Conflict Is, Where It Comes From and How It Climbs
sessions.summary: Before you can calm a conflict you have to read it. Learn what conflict actually is, when it helps and when it hurts, the four sources it grows from, and the escalation ladder that tells you how urgently to act.
objectives: Define workplace conflict and explain why interdependence and perception are at its heart
Distinguish functional from dysfunctional conflict and explain how task conflict turns personal
Classify conflicts by source: task, process, relationship and values, and spot the structural roots behind them
Place a conflict on the escalation ladder and match the stage to the right kind of intervention

cards.title: 143 unread messages
cards.setting: Noor Mithaas Foods head office, Gulberg, Lahore. Six weeks before Eid. 8:40 am.

lines.text: Your promotion to Commercial Operations Lead was announced yesterday. This morning the 'Noor Ops Lahore-Karachi' WhatsApp group shows 143 unread messages.
Karachi left hanging AGAIN. 8,000 Eid gift boxes for our biggest corporate client, promised for the 20th. We got 5,200. On the 23rd. Who exactly is running that plant?
Sales books orders without checking capacity, then blames production. We ran three shifts. Maybe sell what we can actually make?
Maybe make what customers actually buy? Some of us have targets to hit.
Eleven people react with emojis. Someone forwards the thread to the chairman's office.
(voice note) Assalam o alaikum, I'm Farhana Qureshi from People and Culture. Please don't reply in that group yet. Come to my office first, and bring two cups of chai.
This is not just a late order. It is a conflict, and it is climbing. Before we try to fix it, we need to know what kind it is and how high it has already climbed.
Welcome to stage one: the Boiling Kitchen. Let's find out what is really boiling.

scenes.heading: It needs interdependence
scenes.narration: Conflict only happens between people who need each other. Sana needs the plant to deliver, and Bilal needs sales to send workable orders. Strangers can disagree, but they rarely have a conflict.

scenes.heading: It lives in perception
scenes.narration: Conflict starts when one side believes the other is blocking its goals, interests or values. The belief does not have to be accurate. If one person feels blocked, the conflict has already begun.

scenes.heading: Not always bad
scenes.narration: Disagreement about the work itself can produce better decisions. A plant manager who challenges an unrealistic order may save the company from a broken promise.

scenes.heading: Until it turns personal
scenes.narration: Conflict becomes harmful when the focus moves from the problem to the person. Energy goes into winning, blaming and protecting face, and the work suffers.

scenes.heading: Your job as a leader
scenes.narration: Your job is not to remove all conflict. It is to keep it about the work, stop it climbing, and resolve it before it becomes expensive.

cards.title: Functional or dysfunctional?
cards.caption: The same disagreement can sit in either column. What matters is where the energy goes.

items.label: Focus
items.left: The problem, the options and the evidence
items.right: The people, their motives and who is to blame

items.label: Effect on decisions
items.right: Decisions get delayed, made for spite or avoided

items.label: Communication
items.left: Open, direct, in the right forum
items.right: Gossip, sarcasm, side chats and public point-scoring

items.label: Outcome
items.right: Winners, losers and the next round of conflict

cards.question: Which two ingredients must be present for a workplace disagreement to count as a conflict in the sense used in this course?
options: A formal complaint and a manager who has been informed
Two people of equal rank who disagree in public
Raised voices and a breakdown in the relationship
People who depend on each other, and at least one who believes the other is blocking their goals
cards.explanation: Conflict needs interdependence (the parties need each other) and a perceived incompatibility or blocking. It can exist silently, without complaints, shouting or equal rank. Many of the most damaging conflicts are quiet ones.

cards.title: The four sources of conflict
cards.body:
Ask *what are they really disagreeing about?* Most workplace conflicts grow from one of four sources:

- **Task:** the content of the work. What target to set, which product to launch, whether the forecast is right.
- **Process:** how the work gets done. Who decides, who does what, deadlines, procedures and who gets which resources.
- **Relationship:** the people themselves. Perceived disrespect, personality clashes, old grudges, feeling ignored.
- **Values:** deeply held beliefs about what is right or important. Honesty versus loyalty, family versus work time, quality versus speed held as a principle.

Behind these sit **structural roots**: conflicting KPIs, scarce resources, unclear roles, tight interdependence and poor information flow. If you fix only the argument and not the root, it comes back. Fixing the root, for example by giving both sides a shared measure of success, stops the repeats.

cards.title: Name the source
cards.prompt: Match each Noor Mithaas complaint to the source of conflict it shows most clearly.

pairs.right: 'A 10% Eid price rise will kill our volumes.' 'Without it we lose money on every box.'
'Who signs off a rush order: sales, the plant or finance? Nobody seems to know.'
'She never greets me in meetings. She thinks Lahore people are beneath her.'
'I will not tell the client the delay is due to the weather when it isn't.'
Sales is rewarded for volume booked, the plant for low cost per kilo, and neither for on-time delivery.

cards.title: Two stories about one order
cards.setting: Farhana's office. She has Sana on speakerphone from Karachi and Bilal on a video call from the plant.

lines.text: I asked each of you one question: why did the gift-box order fail?
Because Bilal doesn't care about Karachi. He prioritises Lahore orders so his friends in the Lahore sales team look good.
Because Sana books impossible orders to make her numbers, then makes the plant the villain. It's how she operates.
Notice something? Each of you explains the other's behaviour by their character, and your own by the circumstances.
Well... the packaging film did arrive five days late. That wasn't my fault.
And the client did change the box design twice. I couldn't control that.
So we have a task and process problem that is quickly becoming personal. That is the most common way conflict turns toxic.

cards.title: How task conflict turns personal
cards.body:
Research on teams finds that disagreement about the work can help, but relationship conflict almost always hurts. The danger is **spillover**: a task or process disagreement turns into a relationship conflict.

It usually happens through **misattribution**. When someone blocks us, we tend to blame their character ('she is careless', 'he is arrogant'). When we block someone, we point to circumstances ('the film was late'). Psychologists call this tendency to over-blame character the *fundamental attribution error*.

Task disagreement stays healthy when:

- people trust each other's intentions
- the debate happens in the right forum, about evidence
- the leader frames it as 'us against the problem'

**Leader move:** when you hear a judgement about character, ask for the behaviour and the circumstances. 'What exactly happened, and what was going on for them at the time?'

cards.title: Task, process or relationship?
cards.prompt: Sort each line overheard on the shop floor and in the sales office into its main source of conflict.

items.text: 'Our forecast for Eid demand is far too optimistic.'
'Nobody told us the client changed the box design.'
'He rolls his eyes every time I speak.'
'We should use cheaper film to protect the margin.'
'Why does the plant get to set delivery dates without asking sales?'
'She took credit for my idea in front of Haji sahib.'
'Overtime requests sit in finance for a week before anyone approves them.'
'Launching the sugar-free range now is the wrong call.'

cards.title: The escalation ladder
cards.caption: Conflicts climb step by step. The higher they go, the harder and more expensive they are to bring down.

items.label: 1. Friction
items.detail: A difference is noticed. People still talk openly about the issue, if a little tensely.

items.label: 2. Hardening
items.detail: Positions harden. People argue to win, listen selectively and repeat their own case.

items.label: 3. Personalising
items.detail: The other person becomes the problem. Labels, assumed motives, talking about them instead of to them.

items.label: 4. Camps and face
items.detail: Allies are recruited, bosses are copied in, information is withheld and public loss of face hardens everything.

items.label: 5. Open hostility
items.detail: Threats, sabotage, refusal to cooperate. Hurting the other side matters more than the cost to oneself.

cards.title: Watch it climb
cards.prompt: Put these moments from a warehouse dispute in the order the conflict escalated.
steps: The two supervisors disagree about whether the night shift should load trucks early.
Each repeats his own argument in every meeting and stops listening to the other.
One starts calling the other 'lazy' and says he does it to dodge work.
Both copy the general manager on emails and recruit their teams to take sides.
One supervisor quietly delays the other's trucks, even though it hurts the company.

cards.title: Match the stage to the response
cards.body:
The ladder tells you **how** to intervene, not just how worried to be.

| Stage | Typical response |
|---|---|
| 1-2 | The parties can usually sort it out themselves with a nudge: a direct conversation, a clear decision rule, a shared fact base. |
| 3-4 | A third party is needed: a manager acting as facilitator or mediator, private conversations first, then a structured joint meeting. |
| 5 | Facilitation is rarely enough. Senior intervention, a decision imposed, separation of the parties, or a formal HR process. |

A well-known model by researcher Friedrich Glasl has nine stages in three phases: early on **both sides can still win**, in the middle **each tries to win at the other's cost**, and at the end **both accept losing as long as the other loses more**.

**Rule of thumb:** act at the lowest stage you can. Every step up multiplies the cost.

cards.title: The WhatsApp group is on fire
cards.situation: By lunchtime the thread has 210 messages. Sana has posted photos of the half-empty delivery truck, Bilal's shift supervisors are defending him with sarcastic replies, and two Karachi salespeople have written 'typical Lahore'. The chairman's office has seen it all. Farhana asks what you would do first.

choices.text: Post a long, balanced message in the group explaining both sides and asking everyone to calm down.
choices.outcome: Both camps read your message as taking the other side, and 30 more replies follow. Public forums reward point-scoring and face-saving, so a public referee rarely cools a stage 4 conflict.

choices.text: Post one short message moving the discussion out of the group, then call Sana and Bilal separately today to hear each side and set up a joint meeting.
choices.outcome: The thread goes quiet. Each feels heard in private, where nobody has to defend their face in front of their team. This is stage 4 behaviour, so a third party working privately first is the right move.

choices.text: Leave it. Adults should sort out their own disagreements, and stepping in now will look like favouritism.
choices.outcome: By evening the camps are firmer and the client has heard about the 'internal war' from a salesperson. Avoiding can suit trivial stage 1 frictions, not a conflict that is already recruiting allies.

choices.text: Ask the chairman's office to issue a strong instruction that the matter is closed.
choices.outcome: The thread stops, but the anger goes underground and nobody has looked at why the order failed. A power intervention may be needed at stage 5, but here it skips steps that could still work and costs trust.

cards.title: The cost of the gift-box war so far
cards.caption: Farhana's quick estimate for Noor Mithaas. Conflict costs show up in money, time and people long before anyone resigns.

items.label: Order shortfall
items.detail: Of 8,000 promised. The client has asked for a penalty discount on the whole order.

items.label: Management time
items.detail: 6 managers x 5 hours a week x PKR 2,000 an hour x 6 weeks of arguing, chasing and blaming.

items.label: Messages
items.detail: In one WhatsApp thread, read by 40 people, including the chairman's office.

items.label: At-risk talent
items.detail: A shift supervisor and a sales executive have both mentioned looking for other jobs.

cards.front: Myth: a good team has no conflict.
cards.back: Fact: teams with no visible conflict often have hidden conflict or poor decisions. Healthy teams disagree openly about the work and stay respectful.

cards.front: Myth: if nobody complains, there is no conflict.
cards.back: Fact: conflict lives in perception. One person who feels blocked and stays silent can already be withdrawing effort or venting elsewhere.

cards.front: Myth: it's just a personality clash.
cards.back: Fact: many 'personality clashes' are process or structural problems in disguise, such as unclear roles or KPIs that pull in opposite directions.
Fact: unaddressed conflicts tend to climb the ladder. Time helps only if someone uses it to address the cause.

cards.front: Myth: values conflicts can be negotiated like prices.
cards.back: Fact: people rarely trade away core beliefs. Aim for agreement on behaviour and boundaries, not on changing what people believe.

cards.front: Myth: the louder person is the one in conflict.
cards.back: Fact: the quiet party may be further up the ladder: withholding information or recruiting allies out of sight.

cards.question: A finance officer tells you the procurement head 'only delays our approvals to show us who's boss'. The procurement head says finance 'never sends complete documents'. What is the best first diagnostic step?
options: Arrange team-building for both departments to repair the relationship
Decide which head is more senior and support that person's view
Ask both for specific recent examples and check what the approval process actually requires
Treat it as a values conflict, because both believe they are right
cards.explanation: Claims about motives ('to show who's boss') are signs of misattribution. Asking for specific behaviour and checking the process tests whether this is really a process problem dressed up as a relationship one. Team-building on its own treats the symptom.

cards.title: Early warning signs to watch for
cards.body:
Catch conflicts at stage 1 or 2, when they are cheap:

- **Language shifts** from 'the plan' to 'you people', 'always' and 'never'
- **Meeting behaviour:** the same argument repeated, eye-rolling, silence from someone who used to speak
- **Channel shifts:** CC-ing bosses, moving to formal email for small things, side WhatsApp groups
- **Work signs:** information arrives late or not at all, 'not my job' replies
- **Third-party gossip:** you hear about the conflict from someone who isn't in it

When you spot two or more, have a quiet word with each person this week, not next month.

cards.title: Boiling Kitchen cleared
items: Conflict needs interdependence and a perceived blocking of goals, interests or values. It can exist before anyone complains.
Task conflict can improve decisions; relationship conflict almost always harms. Watch for task disputes turning personal through misattribution.
Diagnose the source (task, process, relationship or values) and look for structural roots such as clashing KPIs and unclear roles.
Use the escalation ladder: parties can often self-resolve at stages 1-2, need a third party at 3-4 and usually need senior or formal action at 5.
Conflict has real costs in money, management time and people. Act at the lowest stage you can.

cards.prompt: Think of a disagreement in your own workplace right now. What is its main source, which stage of the ladder has it reached, and what would 'acting at the lowest stage you can' mean this week?

quiz.question: Which of these situations is best described as a workplace conflict rather than a simple difference of opinion?
options: Two sales managers from rival companies argue heatedly at a conference about which pricing strategy works best in Pakistan
A new joiner thinks the office canteen should serve more vegetarian food
Two analysts prefer different spreadsheet layouts for their own private files
A warehouse supervisor who feels the transport team takes his loading bays has begun holding back their schedules
quiz.explanation: The supervisor and transport team depend on each other, and he perceives them as blocking his goals; his behaviour has already changed. The other examples involve no real interdependence or blocked goals, so they are differences of opinion rather than conflicts.

quiz.question: The marketing and finance heads argue about whether to launch a new mango flavour before Eid or wait for a fuller market test. Which source of conflict is this mainly?
options: Task
Relationship
Values
Process
quiz.explanation: The disagreement is about the content of a decision: whether and when to launch. That is task conflict. It would become process conflict if they argued about who has the authority to decide.

quiz.question: Two team leads keep clashing over who should approve customer discounts above 5%. Each thinks it is their call. What is the most likely source of this conflict?
options: Values, because each believes their own judgement is the right one
Process, because the decision right for discounts is unclear
Relationship, because they clearly do not respect each other
Task, because they disagree on the right discount level
quiz.explanation: The argument is about who decides, not what the discount should be. Unclear decision rights are a classic process source. Fixing the approval rule will usually remove the friction.

quiz.question: A senior manager believes committed staff never leave before the boss does. A younger team member believes output matters, not hours at the desk, and leaves on time daily. Which description fits best?
options: A values conflict about what commitment means; agreeing expected behaviour beats trying to change beliefs
A task conflict about workload and working hours that a clearer shift schedule and a fair overtime policy would fully solve
A process conflict about attendance rules that only HR can settle
A relationship conflict, because they dislike each other personally
quiz.explanation: Each holds a deep belief about what a good employee is. Values are rarely traded away, so the practical route is to agree clear expectations on hours, availability and output, rather than trying to convert either person.

quiz.question: In a dispute between two shift supervisors, each has started calling the other 'careless' and 'political' and they now complain about each other to colleagues instead of talking directly. Which stage of the escalation ladder have they most clearly reached?
options: Friction
Hardening
Personalising
Open hostility
quiz.explanation: Labels, assumed motives and talking about rather than to the other person are signs of personalising (stage 3). They have not yet formed camps or moved to threats and sabotage.

quiz.question: Why do task disagreements so often turn into relationship conflicts?
options: Because task conflict is always harmful and spreads by its nature
Because relationship conflict is easier to resolve, so people move to it
Because managers usually take sides in task disagreements, which leaves the losing side feeling personally attacked
Because people tend to blame the other side's character but their own circumstances
quiz.explanation: Misattribution, often called the fundamental attribution error, makes us read the other side's blocking as a character flaw. That turns 'the plan is wrong' into 'he is the problem'. Task conflict itself can be useful.

quiz.question: Which sign best shows that a disagreement is still functional?
options: Nobody disagrees openly in meetings any more, and decisions are reached quickly and politely
The argument has moved to a private WhatsApp group
One side has agreed to stay silent to keep the peace
Both sides debate the evidence and stay committed to the final decision
quiz.explanation: Functional conflict focuses on the problem and the evidence and ends in shared ownership of the decision. Silence and moving to side channels are signs of avoidance or escalation, not health.

quiz.question: Sales staff are rewarded for volume booked, while the plant is rewarded for low cost per kilo. Neither is measured on on-time delivery. What does this create?
options: A structural root that will keep producing disputes until the measures change
A relationship conflict between individual managers that needs coaching for both department heads
A values conflict about quality
A functional conflict that should be left alone
quiz.explanation: Clashing KPIs are a structural root. Sales is pushed to book more; the plant is pushed to avoid costly rush runs. Resolving one argument will not stop the next until the incentives are aligned, for example with a shared on-time-in-full measure.

quiz.question: In Friedrich Glasl's well-known escalation model, what characterises the final phase?
options: Both sides can still find a solution where both win
Both sides accept losing themselves as long as the other side loses more
Each side openly tries to win at the other's expense and recruits allies to help it
The parties agree to call in a mediator
quiz.explanation: Glasl's nine stages group into three phases: win-win, then win-lose, then lose-lose, where damaging the other side matters more than one's own losses.

quiz.question: Four managers each spend about 6 hours a week on an unresolved dispute (meetings, chasing and complaining). Their average cost to the company is PKR 2,500 an hour. What is the management-time cost over 4 weeks?
quiz.explanation: 4 managers x 6 hours = 24 hours a week. 24 x PKR 2,500 = PKR 60,000 a week. Over 4 weeks: PKR 240,000. PKR 60,000 is the weekly figure only.

sessions.title: The Five Conflict-Handling Modes and When Each Fits
sessions.summary: Everyone has a favourite way of handling conflict, and most of us overuse it. Learn the five modes, the two dimensions behind them, the situations each one suits and the price of overusing or avoiding each.
objectives: Describe the five conflict-handling modes using the dimensions of assertiveness and cooperativeness
Choose the mode that best fits a situation using importance, relationship, time, power and need for commitment
Recognise the signs and costs of overusing or underusing each mode
Identify your own default mode and plan how to stretch beyond it

cards.title: The rule nobody asked for
cards.setting: Boardroom, Noor Mithaas head office, Lahore. Monday management meeting.

lines.text: I've solved the gift-box problem. From today, no rush order is accepted without my personal sign-off. Done.
With respect, Danish, Karachi clients decide in hours, not days. This rule will cost us the season. We need to discuss it properly.
(looking at his phone) Whatever is decided is fine with the plant.
Beta, let's not fight in front of everyone. If Danish thinks it's best, we go with it. Sana, adjust a little.
After the meeting, Farhana catches you in the corridor.
Did you notice? Four people, four different ways of handling the same conflict. Danish forced, Sana fought back, Bilal checked out and Haji sahib smoothed it over.
None of those is wrong in every situation. The skill is choosing the right one on purpose. Stage two is the Five Doors. Let's open them.

scenes.heading: Dial one: assertiveness
scenes.narration: The first dial is how hard you push for your own concerns. Turned up, you state your needs and stand firm. Turned down, you set your own goals aside.

scenes.heading: Dial two: cooperativeness
scenes.narration: The second dial is how much you try to meet the other person's concerns. Turned up, you work for their needs. Turned down, their needs are not your problem.

scenes.heading: Five combinations
scenes.narration: Combine the dials and you get five doors. Push hard and ignore them: competing. Push hard and help them too: collaborating. Push for neither: avoiding. Help them and drop your own: accommodating. Middle on both: compromising.

scenes.heading: A widely used model
scenes.narration: This way of mapping conflict behaviour was made popular by researchers Kenneth Thomas and Ralph Kilmann. It describes behaviour in a situation, not a fixed personality.

scenes.heading: No single best door
scenes.narration: Every door is right somewhere. Collaborating is powerful but slow. Competing is fast but costly to trust. Skilled leaders pick the door that fits the moment.

cards.title: The five-mode map
cards.caption: Compromising sits in the centre: some assertiveness and some cooperativeness, so each side gets part of what it wants.

items.label: Competing
items.detail: High assertiveness, low cooperativeness. 'My way, for good reasons.'

items.label: Collaborating
items.detail: High on both. 'Let's find a solution that fully works for both of us.'

items.label: Avoiding
items.detail: Low on both. 'Not now, or not me.'

items.label: Accommodating
items.detail: Low assertiveness, high cooperativeness. 'Your way this time.'

cards.back: Pursuing your own concern firmly, even at the other's expense. Uses authority, argument or position. Right for emergencies and non-negotiables.
Digging beneath both sides' positions to find a solution that fully meets both sets of needs. Takes time and trust.
Finding a quick, acceptable middle where each side gives up something. Expedient, but nobody is fully satisfied.
Sidestepping, postponing or withdrawing from the issue. Neither side's concern is addressed for now.
Setting aside your own concern to satisfy the other's. Generous, and wise when the issue matters far more to them.

cards.front: Is a mode a personality type?
cards.back: No. Everyone can use all five. Most people have one or two defaults they overuse under pressure.

cards.question: What is the key difference between collaborating and compromising?
options: Collaborating is used by senior managers, compromising by junior staff
There is no real difference; both are cooperative
Compromising takes longer because both sides must give something up
Collaborating looks for a solution that fully meets both sides' needs; compromising splits the difference so each side gets part
cards.explanation: Collaborating is high on both dials and aims to satisfy both sides fully, usually by exploring underlying needs. Compromising is moderate on both and settles for a middle point. Compromising is usually quicker, not slower.

cards.title: When each door fits, and its price

items.label: Competing
items.left: Emergencies, safety, legal or ethical lines, unpopular but vital decisions
items.right: Resentment, low commitment, people stop raising problems

items.label: Collaborating
items.left: Issue too important to split, long-term relationship, buy-in needed, time available
items.right: Slow decisions, meeting fatigue, energy wasted on trivia

items.label: Compromising
items.left: Equal power, moderate stakes, time pressure, a temporary fix, or when collaborating has failed
items.right: Half-solutions, creative options missed, principles split

items.label: Avoiding
items.left: Trivial issue, tempers need cooling, more facts needed, someone else should resolve it
items.right: Issues fester, decisions made by default, leader seen as weak

items.label: Accommodating
items.left: You are wrong, the issue matters more to them, building goodwill, harmony is key
items.right: Own needs unmet, quiet resentment, seen as a pushover

cards.title: Pick the door
cards.prompt: Match each Noor Mithaas situation to the mode that fits it best.

pairs.right: A worker removes a machine guard to speed up packing. You stop the line immediately.
Designing a new order-to-delivery process with sales and the plant for the next three years.
Lahore and Karachi each want the one refrigerated truck on Friday. Each gets it for half the day.
Two clerks bicker over which brand of tea the pantry stocks. You leave it to them.
Bilal shows you that your proposed shift pattern breaks the labour rota. You adopt his version.

cards.title: Choosing a door: five questions
cards.body:
Before you respond in a conflict, ask yourself:

1. **How important is the issue to me** (and to the organisation)?
2. **How important is the relationship**, now and in future?
3. **How much time** do we have?
4. **What is the power balance?** Who can decide, and who must live with it?
5. **Do I need their commitment** to make the outcome work?

Rough patterns:

- High issue + high relationship + time + commitment needed: **collaborate**
- High issue + urgent or non-negotiable: **compete** (and explain afterwards)
- Moderate issue + equal power + time pressure: **compromise**
- Low issue for you + high for them: **accommodate**
- Low issue, or the wrong time or wrong person: **avoid** (for now)

cards.title: Behind closed doors
cards.setting: Farhana's office. Sana and Bilal have each come in separately during the afternoon.

lines.text: I fought Danish in the meeting because nobody else would. If I don't push, Karachi always loses.
And how often does pushing hard work for you?
...With clients, often. With the plant, it just makes Bilal dig in.
(later) I stayed quiet because arguing with the owner's son is pointless. But this rule will jam my planning. Rush orders will arrive with no warning after his sign-off.
So you avoided, and you're carrying a problem nobody knows about. That's the price of the avoiding door.
And Haji sahib accommodated his son to keep the peace. Now you, our new lead, have to choose your door with Danish. Which one?

cards.title: Your move with Danish
cards.situation: Danish's sign-off rule starts tomorrow. You believe a rush-order rule is needed, but his version will delay Karachi and give the plant no warning. Danish is the founder's son and a director. The order-to-delivery process will run for years, and you need both Sana and Bilal to support whatever is decided. You have about a week before Eid orders peak.

choices.text: Accept the rule quietly. He is a director, and challenging the family is risky for a new lead.
choices.outcome: You keep the peace, but Karachi loses two orders that week and Bilal's planning chaos continues. Accommodating suits issues that matter little to you; this one matters a great deal to the business.

choices.text: Ask Danish for 30 minutes with Sana and Bilal to design a rush-order rule together that protects margins, speed and plant planning.
choices.outcome: Danish agrees once you frame it as making his idea work. In one session the group builds a rule with capacity checks and a two-hour approval window. High stakes, a long-term process and the need for commitment from both sides make collaborating the right door.

choices.text: Propose a quick middle ground: Danish signs off orders over PKR 1 million, Sana approves the rest.
choices.outcome: It's faster than the original rule and Danish accepts it, but nobody has asked Bilal about capacity, so the plant problem remains. A compromise can buy time, but it misses the underlying needs here.

choices.text: Email the chairman explaining why Danish's rule is wrong and ask him to overrule his son.
choices.outcome: Haji sahib is embarrassed and Danish feels ambushed. Even if the rule changes, you have made a powerful enemy. Competing through a higher authority costs trust you will need for years.

cards.title: Collaborate, compromise or avoid for now?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation into the mode that fits it best.

items.text: Designing a five-year distribution agreement with your largest distributor
Two equal teams want the same conference room at 3 pm today; you can split the hour
A colleague is furious and shouting; you suggest talking after lunch
Merging the Lahore and Karachi customer databases, where both teams' knowledge matters
A brief dispute over the font on the internal newsletter
A union and management agree a temporary overtime rate until the full wage review
A disagreement between two other departments that their own head is already handling
Setting shared quality standards that both R&D and the plant must live with

cards.title: The overtime budget
cards.body:
At Noor Mithaas's Lahore plant, the Eid overtime budget is PKR 2.4 million. Bilal wants PKR 1.8 million for packing; the dispatch supervisor wants PKR 1.2 million for loading. That's PKR 600,000 more than exists.

**First try: compromise.** Split the shortfall: each gives up PKR 300,000. Packing gets PKR 1.5m, dispatch PKR 0.9m. Quick, but both now say they cannot hit their numbers.

**Second try: collaborate.** Farhana asks *why* each needs the money. Packing's peak is days 1-10; dispatch's is days 8-20. Only three days overlap. By staggering the overtime rota and sharing six packers who can load trucks, the plant covers both peaks for PKR 2.3 million.

**Lesson:** compromise divided the budget. Collaboration found that the needs weren't really in competition. When time allows and the stakes are real, try collaborating before you split the difference.

cards.question: A manager uses the competing mode in almost every disagreement. Which warning sign would you most expect to see in the team?
options: Long meetings where every decision takes weeks
Team members stop raising problems and quietly comply
The manager's own needs are rarely met
Small issues are left to fester without decisions
cards.explanation: Overusing competing teaches people that speaking up is pointless, so problems surface late and commitment drops. Slow decisions point to overused collaborating, unmet own needs to overused accommodating and festering issues to overused avoiding.

cards.title: Know your default, then stretch
cards.body:
Under pressure, most of us fall back on one or two favourite modes.

- **Find your default:** think of your last three conflicts. Which door did you walk through each time?
- **Ask a trusted colleague** which mode you use too much. They usually know.
- **Stretch one notch:** if you avoid, practise stating one need clearly. If you compete, practise asking one genuine question before deciding.
- **Say your mode out loud:** 'This one is a safety line, so I'm deciding now and will explain after' turns competing into a respected choice.

A default mode is a habit, not a destiny.

cards.title: Five Doors opened
items: The five modes come from two dials: assertiveness (your concerns) and cooperativeness (their concerns).
Competing for emergencies and non-negotiables; collaborating for important, long-term issues that need buy-in; compromising for moderate, time-pressured issues between equals.
Avoiding suits trivial issues, cooling-off time, missing facts or someone else's problem; accommodating suits issues that matter more to them or when you are wrong.
Choose using five questions: issue importance, relationship importance, time, power and need for commitment.
Every mode has a price when overused. Know your default and stretch deliberately.

cards.prompt: Which of the five doors do you walk through most often under pressure? Recall one recent conflict where a different door would have worked better, and describe what you would have said.

quiz.question: Which conflict-handling mode combines high assertiveness with low cooperativeness?
options: Collaborating
Accommodating
Compromising
Competing
quiz.explanation: Competing means pursuing your own concerns firmly with little attention to the other side's. Collaborating is high on both dials; accommodating is the reverse of competing.

quiz.question: A manager says: 'Let's each explain what we really need from this budget and look for a plan that gives both teams everything essential.' Which mode is she using?
options: Collaborating
Compromising
Accommodating
Avoiding
quiz.explanation: Exploring both sides' underlying needs to find a solution that fully satisfies both is collaborating. Compromising would accept a middle point where each side gives something up.

quiz.question: During a night shift, a supervisor sees a forklift driver loading pallets with a damaged mast. The driver argues that the order must leave by 6 am. Which mode should the supervisor use?
options: Compromising: allow half the pallets to be loaded with the damaged forklift
Competing: stop the forklift immediately and explain the reasons afterwards
Collaborating: hold a discussion to find a solution that meets both concerns
Accommodating: let the driver continue because the order is urgent
quiz.explanation: A safety risk calls for quick, firm action, which is when competing fits. A discussion can follow once the risk is removed, for example about finding another forklift. Splitting the difference on safety is not acceptable.

quiz.question: In a planning meeting you argue for your shift pattern, but a colleague shows convincingly that it breaks the legal rest-hours rule. What is the most appropriate mode?
options: Accommodating
Competing
Avoiding
Compromising
quiz.explanation: When you realise you are wrong, accommodating, by accepting the better proposal, is right. It also shows you are reasonable, which builds credibility for later disagreements.

quiz.question: Two department heads of equal rank both want the only company van on Saturday. Each has a moderately important job, there is no time for a long discussion and no other vehicle is available. Which mode fits best?
options: Collaborating
Compromising
Competing
Avoiding
quiz.explanation: Equal power, moderate stakes and time pressure are the classic conditions for compromising, for example a morning and afternoon split. Collaborating would take more time than the issue deserves.

quiz.question: A colleague storms into your office shouting about a decision. You say: 'I can see this matters a lot. Let's sit down together at 3 pm when I can give it full attention.' Which statement about this response is most accurate?
options: It is accommodating, because you are giving the colleague exactly what he wants: your full attention
It is a poor response, because conflicts should always be addressed immediately
It is competing, because you are controlling the timing
A deliberate, temporary use of avoiding to let tempers cool, with a time to return
quiz.explanation: Postponing when emotions are high is a valid use of avoiding. Setting a specific time to return stops it from becoming the harmful kind of avoiding where the issue is never addressed.

quiz.question: A team leader almost always gives in to other departments' requests to keep relationships smooth. Her team is overloaded and increasingly frustrated. Which mode is she overusing?
options: Avoiding
Compromising
Accommodating
Collaborating
quiz.explanation: Consistently setting aside her own (and her team's) concerns to satisfy others is overused accommodating. Its price is unmet needs and quiet resentment.

quiz.question: Which combination of factors most strongly points to collaborating?
options: An important issue, a long-term relationship, enough time and a need for commitment
A trivial issue, little time and a one-off relationship
An emergency where quick action is vital
Equal power on both sides, moderate stakes for each and a firm deadline less than an hour away
quiz.explanation: Collaborating takes time and energy, so it is worth it when the issue and relationship both matter and you need real commitment. Emergencies call for competing; equal power under time pressure suits compromising.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of overusing the avoiding mode as a manager?
options: Team members stop raising problems because they fear being overruled every time they speak up
Issues fester, decisions are made by default and the manager is seen as weak
Decisions take too long because everyone must agree
The manager builds too much goodwill with other departments
quiz.explanation: Avoiding leaves concerns unaddressed, so problems grow and others decide by default. Fear of being overruled is the price of overused competing, and slow consensus is the price of overused collaborating.

quiz.question: Which statement about the five conflict-handling modes is most accurate?
options: Collaborating is always the best mode, and the other four are only fallbacks for when it fails
Each person has one fixed mode linked to their personality
Each mode suits some situations; skilled people choose deliberately and know their default
Compromising is the most professional mode because it is fair to both sides
quiz.explanation: The modes describe behaviour, not fixed personality. Each fits certain conditions and has a price when overused. Collaborating is powerful but slow and wasteful on trivial issues.

sessions.title: Emotions, De-escalation and Difficult Conversations
sessions.summary: Conflict is hot. Learn what anger does to your brain and body, how to steady yourself, how to bring a heated person down, how to set a respectful boundary and how to prepare and hold the difficult conversation you have been avoiding.
objectives: Explain the threat response and why strong emotion narrows thinking
Use self-regulation techniques: pausing, slow breathing, naming the emotion and reframing
De-escalate a heated colleague or customer and set a respectful boundary when behaviour crosses a line
Prepare and hold a difficult conversation using the three layers, intent versus impact and Situation-Behaviour-Impact

cards.title: The call that exploded
cards.setting: Video call between the Lahore plant office and the Karachi sales hub. Five weeks to Eid.

lines.text: The new rush-order rule is working, but Karachi is still getting the last slots on every production run. Again.
(slamming the table) Because you send orders at 6 pm for next-morning delivery! Do you think my workers are machines?!
Don't you dare shout at me. I've had enough of this plant's attitude!
Bilal's face is red. Sana's camera goes off. Two plant supervisors are watching from the doorway behind Bilal.
(joining the call) Let's stop here. I can see both of you are very frustrated, and this matters a lot to both of you. We will pick this up at 4 pm.
(to you, after the call) When people are this hot, nobody can think. Before you can resolve anything, you need to cool the room, and yourself.
Stage three: the Cooling Room. And at the end, you are going to hold a conversation you would rather avoid.

scenes.heading: The alarm goes off
scenes.narration: When we feel threatened, by a shout, an insult or a public embarrassment, the brain's alarm system reacts before our thinking brain has caught up. It prepares us to fight, flee or freeze.

scenes.heading: The body joins in
scenes.narration: Heart rate climbs, breathing gets shallow, muscles tense and attention narrows onto the threat. Great for escaping danger. Terrible for a planning meeting.

scenes.heading: Thinking goes foggy
scenes.narration: In this state we listen less, remember less and say things we regret. Some writers call it an 'amygdala hijack': the alarm system takes the controls.

scenes.heading: Cooling takes time
scenes.narration: The body calms down more slowly than it heats up. After a big surge, a meaningful break, often twenty minutes or more, works far better than a two-minute pause.

scenes.heading: You can turn it down
scenes.narration: Slow breathing with a longer out-breath, naming the emotion and stepping away all help the thinking brain take back control. That is emotional regulation.

cards.title: Steady yourself: the PAUSE routine
cards.caption: Use it the moment you notice the heat rising: in a meeting, on the phone or before you hit send.

items.label: Notice
items.detail: Catch the body signals: hot face, tight jaw, racing heart, the urge to interrupt.

items.label: Pause
items.detail: Stop before reacting. Take a sip of water, look at your notes, or ask for a short break.

items.label: Breathe
items.detail: Slow breaths with a longer exhale, for example in for four counts and out for six.

items.label: Name it
items.detail: Label the feeling silently: 'I'm feeling humiliated.' Naming an emotion tends to reduce its intensity.

items.label: Reframe
items.detail: Ask: what else could explain their behaviour? What do I actually want from this conversation?

items.label: Choose
items.detail: Respond on purpose: a question, a summary, a boundary or a request to continue later.

cards.question: Why is it usually a mistake to push for a solution while both people are still very angry?
options: Because the threat response narrows attention and reduces the ability to listen and think flexibly
Because anger is unprofessional and should be punished first
Because angry people always want to compromise
Because solutions agreed in anger are legally invalid
cards.explanation: Strong emotion triggers the threat response, which narrows attention and weakens listening and complex thinking. Cooling first gives a better chance of a solution both sides can stick to.

cards.title: Phrases that inflame, phrases that cool

cards.back: Implies their feelings are wrong, so it usually inflames. Try: 'I can see this is really frustrating. Help me understand what happened.'
Sounds like a wall. Try: 'Here's what I can do within our rules, and here's why the rule exists.'
Generalisations invite a defence of the exceptions. Try: 'In the last two orders, the change came after 6 pm.'
Signals disrespect is coming. Try simply: 'I see it differently. Can I explain why?'
Denial makes people distrust you. Try owning it: 'I'm frustrated, and I want to sort this out properly.'
Signals withdrawal, not agreement. Try: 'I need a few minutes to think. Can we continue at 4?'

cards.title: Bringing someone down from the heat
cards.caption: Start wide by making the person feel safe and heard, then narrow towards a solution. Skipping to the bottom too early sends them back up.

items.label: Safety and space
items.detail: Move to a private place, sit down if possible, lower your voice and slow your pace.

items.label: Listen
items.detail: Let them speak without interrupting, defending or correcting details yet.

items.label: Acknowledge
items.detail: Name the emotion and the reason: 'You're angry because the plan changed without warning.'

items.label: Clarify
items.detail: Ask open questions and summarise the facts until they agree you've understood.

items.label: Options and agreement
items.detail: Offer choices and agree a next step, ideally with a time.

cards.title: Bilal on the plant floor
cards.situation: At 3 pm you visit the plant to prepare for the 4 pm call. Bilal sees you and starts loudly: 'Are you here to blame me too? Sales sends garbage orders and I get the shouting!' Several workers stop to watch. He is red-faced but not threatening, and he is a respected senior manager.

choices.text: 'Bilal, calm down. Let's be professional. You can't shout in front of the workers.'
choices.outcome: He gets louder: now he is being lectured in front of his own team. 'Calm down' and a public correction threaten his face and push him further up the heat.

choices.text: 'I'm not here to blame anyone. You've been taking the heat for problems that aren't all yours. Can we talk in your office? I want to hear it properly.'
choices.outcome: He exhales and leads you to his office. You acknowledged his frustration and its cause, offered privacy and showed you wanted to listen. That brings him down the funnel.

choices.text: Explain calmly, right there, that the 6 pm orders came from a client, not from Sana.
choices.outcome: The facts are right but the timing is wrong. He hears a defence of Sana in front of his team and argues harder. Correct details only after the person feels heard.

choices.text: Say nothing, turn around and come back tomorrow.
choices.outcome: He reads it as contempt, and the story spreads that the new lead walked out on him. Leaving can be right when someone is abusive or threatening, but here a respectful offer to talk would have worked.

cards.title: When to set a boundary
cards.body:
Acknowledging emotion does not mean accepting any behaviour. If someone keeps shouting, swears at you or insults you **after** you have listened and acknowledged, set a boundary: calm, specific and with a way forward.

> 'I want to help sort this out. I can't continue while there's shouting. Let's take fifteen minutes and meet again in the conference room.'

Good boundaries:

- describe the behaviour, not the person's character
- say what you will do, not only what they must stop
- offer a clear route back to the conversation

**Safety comes first.** If there is any threat of violence, do not stay alone with the person. Move away, get help from security or colleagues, and report it. That is no longer a conflict to mediate; it is a safety and disciplinary matter.

cards.title: The conversation you're avoiding
cards.setting: Farhana's office, 5:30 pm. The 4 pm call went better. Everyone is tired.

lines.text: Good work today. Bilal apologised for shouting, and Sana accepted. But there's one more thing, and it's yours.
Sana's public WhatsApp posts started this fire. And her 'typical Lahore' comment hurt the whole plant team. Someone has to talk to her.
Your stomach tightens. Sana is your best-performing sales manager, and she already feels Karachi is treated unfairly.
Most people either avoid this conversation or charge in with an accusation. We're going to prepare it properly.
Every difficult conversation is really three conversations at once. Let's map them.

cards.title: Three conversations in one
cards.caption: The visible argument is about facts. Underneath sit feelings, and deepest of all, what the situation means about who we are.

items.label: What happened
items.detail: Who did what, who meant what, who is to blame. Usually where people argue.

items.label: Feelings
items.detail: Hurt, anger, embarrassment, anxiety. Often unspoken, but steering everything.

items.label: Identity
items.detail: What this says about me: Am I competent? A good person? Respected? Help by being clear about what you are and aren't saying.

cards.title: Intent, impact and contribution
cards.body:
Two shifts make the 'what happened' conversation far less defensive.

**1. Separate intent from impact.** We know our own intentions, but we only guess at theirs, usually badly. Talk about the **impact** on you and ask about their **intent** rather than assuming it.

> Instead of 'You wanted to humiliate the plant', try 'When the photos were posted, the plant team felt humiliated. What were you hoping to achieve?'

**2. Map contribution, not blame.** Blame looks backwards and asks who is guilty. Contribution asks what each person, including you, did that helped create the situation, so you can change it.

> 'I contributed too: I never set a rule for where we discuss delivery problems.'

Admitting your own contribution first often lowers the other person's defences.

cards.title: Build feedback with Situation-Behaviour-Impact
cards.prompt: Match each part of the Situation-Behaviour-Impact model to the line you might use with Sana.

pairs.right: 'On Tuesday morning, in the Noor Ops WhatsApp group...'
'...you posted photos of the half-empty truck and wrote "typical Lahore"...'
'...the plant team felt publicly humiliated, and three supervisors stopped replying to Karachi's messages.'
'I'd like to understand what was going on for you, and agree how we raise problems from now on.'

cards.title: Observation or judgement?
cards.prompt: Good feedback describes behaviour you could film. Sort each statement.

items.text: 'You posted the photos in a group of 40 people.'
'You were being unprofessional.'
'You interrupted Bilal three times in the meeting.'
'You obviously don't respect the plant.'
'The order change reached the plant at 6:10 pm.'
'You have an attitude problem.'
'You switched off your camera and left the call.'
'You were trying to make the plant look bad.'

cards.title: Running the difficult conversation
cards.prompt: Put the stages of a well-run difficult conversation in order.
steps: Prepare: clarify your purpose, the facts, your feelings and what might be at stake for the other person.
Open with a neutral 'third story': describe the difference as a fair observer would, and invite them in.
Explore their view first: ask, listen and summarise until they feel understood.
Share your view: use Situation-Behaviour-Impact and speak about your own feelings and contribution.
Problem-solve together: generate options and agree specific next steps.
Follow up: check in after an agreed time to see whether the agreement is working.

cards.question: Which opening line is the best example of a neutral 'third story' for your conversation with Sana?
options: 'Sana, your WhatsApp posts were completely out of line.'
'Sana, I'm sure you didn't mean anything by it, so let's just forget Tuesday.'
'Sana, it seems you and the plant see the delivery problems very differently, and Tuesday's posts landed badly there. I'd like us to understand each other's view and agree how to raise problems.'
'Sana, Farhana asked me to speak to you about your behaviour.'
cards.explanation: A third story describes the difference without taking either side's version as the truth, names the issue honestly and invites a shared purpose. The other options accuse, avoid or hide behind someone else.

cards.title: How the conversation with Sana went
cards.body:
You meet Sana in a quiet room with tea, not in your office.

**Opening (third story):** 'I think you and the plant see the delivery problems very differently, and Tuesday's posts landed badly in Lahore. I'd like to understand your side and agree how we raise problems from now on.'

**Exploring:** Sana says she posted because her emails to the plant went unanswered for days. 'I felt invisible. My client was shouting at me.' You summarise: 'So you went public because private channels weren't working, and you were under real pressure.' She nods.

**Your view (SBI):** you describe the posts and the impact on the supervisors. You add your own contribution: 'I never set up a proper escalation route.'

**Agreement:** delivery problems go to a daily 15-minute call, not the group. Sana will message the supervisors directly to clear the air. You will check in after a week.

Identity mattered: Sana needed to hear she was valued, not that she was a troublemaker.

cards.title: Hot moments on WhatsApp and email
cards.body:
Written conflict escalates faster: no tone of voice, no faces, and a permanent record.

- **Never reply while hot.** Write the draft in your notes app, not in the chat, and wait at least until you have calmed down.
- **Move it offline:** 'Let's discuss this on a call at 11' beats ten more messages.
- **One issue per message,** facts first, no sarcasm, no capital letters.
- **Praise in public, address problems in private.** Never correct someone in a group.
- **Voice notes** can soften tone but can also be forwarded. Speak as if your chairman will hear it.

cards.title: Cooling Room cleared
items: The threat response narrows attention and weakens thinking; cool down before problem-solving, and allow a meaningful break after a big surge.
Regulate yourself: notice, pause, breathe slowly, name the emotion, reframe and choose your response.
De-escalate others: safety and privacy, listen, acknowledge the emotion and its cause, clarify, then offer options. Avoid 'calm down' and public corrections.
Set calm, specific boundaries when behaviour crosses a line, and treat any threat of violence as a safety matter.
Difficult conversations have three layers: what happened, feelings and identity. Open with a third story, separate intent from impact, map contribution and use Situation-Behaviour-Impact.

cards.prompt: Which conversation have you been avoiding at work? Write the neutral 'third story' opening line you could use, and one thing you contributed to the situation that you could admit first.

quiz.question: What typically happens to a person's thinking during a strong threat response in a heated argument?
options: Attention widens and the person weighs up more options, because the stakes feel so much higher
Memory improves because the situation feels important
The person becomes more creative and persuasive
Attention narrows onto the threat and the capacity to listen and think flexibly drops
quiz.explanation: The threat response prepares the body to fight, flee or freeze. Attention narrows and complex thinking and listening suffer, which is why decisions made in anger are often poor.

quiz.question: In a tense meeting you notice your face getting hot and you silently tell yourself, 'I'm feeling embarrassed.' What is the main benefit of this step?
options: Naming an emotion tends to reduce its intensity, helping you think clearly
It shows the other person that you are weak
It removes the need to take a break later, because the feeling has now been fully dealt with
It guarantees the other person will calm down too
quiz.explanation: Labelling an emotion, even silently, tends to reduce its intensity. It is part of the PAUSE routine. It doesn't guarantee anything about the other person, and you may still need a break.

quiz.question: A distributor calls, shouting that his stock arrived damaged for the second time. Which response is most likely to de-escalate?
options: 'Please calm down, sir, there's no need to shout.'
'I'm sorry, sir, but that isn't our fault; the courier company handles all transport, so let me give you their complaints number.'
'Our policy says complaints must be made by email.'
'Damaged stock twice, right before Eid, is really frustrating. Tell me what arrived and I'll check options now.'
quiz.explanation: Acknowledging the emotion and its cause, then moving to clarifying facts, follows the de-escalation funnel. 'Calm down', blame-shifting and hiding behind policy usually raise the heat.

quiz.question: You have listened to and acknowledged an angry colleague, but he keeps shouting and has started swearing at you. What should you do?
options: Keep listening silently for as long as it takes, because interrupting an angry person always makes things worse
Set a calm boundary: you can't continue while he shouts, and you'll meet again after a short break
Shout back so he knows you won't be pushed around
Report him for misconduct immediately without saying anything
quiz.explanation: Once you have acknowledged the person, continued abuse calls for a boundary that names the behaviour, says what you will do and offers a way back. Shouting back escalates it, and endless silence lets the behaviour continue.

quiz.question: Which statement follows the Situation-Behaviour-Impact model best?
options: 'You're always so careless with client deadlines, and this keeps happening even though we have discussed it many times.'
'I feel you don't take your job seriously.'
'In Monday's client call, you promised Friday shipping without checking with the plant; the client has now complained.'
'Everyone has noticed your attitude recently.'
quiz.explanation: It names a specific situation (Monday's call), an observable behaviour (promising Friday without checking) and the impact (a client complaint). The others are judgements or generalisations.

quiz.question: A colleague says, 'You deliberately left me out of the client meeting to take the credit.' You did not intend that at all. What is the most constructive reply?
options: 'I didn't intend that, but I can see being left out hurt. Can you tell me more about the impact?'
'That's ridiculous. I would never do that.'
'You're being too sensitive.'
'If you had been at your desk when the meeting started, I would certainly have invited you to join us.'
quiz.explanation: Separating intent from impact means stating your intent honestly without dismissing the impact on them. Denial, labelling them as oversensitive or counter-blame keep the argument stuck on who is guilty.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of opening a difficult conversation with a 'third story'?
options: To present your own version of events as clearly and persuasively as possible, before the other side does
To tell a story that lightens the mood before the real issue
To bring in a third person as a witness
To describe the difference as a neutral observer would, so neither version is assumed true
quiz.explanation: A third story names the issue in a way both people could accept, which lowers defensiveness and invites joint problem-solving. It isn't about witnesses or ice-breakers.

quiz.question: After opening a difficult conversation, what should normally come next?
options: Present your solution so the conversation stays short
List all the evidence you have collected, so the facts are clear before anyone gives an opinion
Explore the other person's view, listening and summarising until they feel understood
Ask them to apologise before continuing
quiz.explanation: Exploring their view first lowers defensiveness and often reveals facts you did not know. Jumping to solutions or evidence too early sends people back up the heat.

quiz.question: When you give a high-performing analyst feedback about a careless error, she reacts strongly: 'So now I'm incompetent?' Which layer of the conversation has been triggered?
options: What happened
Identity
Feelings
Process
quiz.explanation: Her reaction is about what the feedback says about who she is: competent or not. That is the identity layer. Being clear about what you are and are not saying ('one error, not your overall ability') helps.

quiz.question: Which approach best reflects 'mapping contribution' rather than assigning blame?
options: Working out which person caused the problem, so that they can be held fully accountable for it
Identifying what each person, including you, did to create the situation, so it can change
Agreeing that nobody is responsible so that everyone feels better
Asking a senior manager to decide who was at fault
quiz.explanation: Contribution looks forward: each person's part, including your own, shows what to change. Blame looks backward for one guilty party and makes people defensive. It is not the same as saying nobody is responsible.

sessions.title: Interest-Based Negotiation and Mediation for Managers
sessions.summary: Move from fighting over positions to solving for interests. Learn interest-based negotiation, how to work out your BATNA, walk-away point and the zone of possible agreement, and a step-by-step mediation method for settling disputes between your people.
objectives: Distinguish positions from interests and uncover the interests behind a demand
Apply the four elements of interest-based negotiation, including objective criteria
Calculate a BATNA-based walk-away point and the zone of possible agreement
Run a mediation between two colleagues: preparation, joint meeting, interests, options, written agreement and follow-up

cards.title: Two ultimatums in one morning
cards.setting: Your desk, Noor Mithaas head office. Four weeks to Eid. 9:15 am.

lines.text: Bad news. Shahrah Traders, our main Karachi distributor, wants their margin raised from 11% to 14%. Otherwise they switch to a rival brand before Eid.
14%? Absolutely not. Tell them we'll find another distributor. Nobody threatens Noor Mithaas.
And while you're at it: Sana now wants the first production slot every Monday, guaranteed. That will wreck my changeover plan. The answer is no.
Without that slot, Karachi's Tuesday corporate deliveries arrive stale. The answer has to be yes.
Two negotiations, four people, and everyone is shouting a position. Nobody has said what they actually need.
Stage four is the Negotiation Table. You'll learn to negotiate on interests, then mediate between Sana and Bilal yourself.

scenes.heading: Positions are walls
scenes.narration: A position is what someone says they want: '14% margin', 'the Monday slot', 'no fixed slots'. Positions are concrete, and they clash.

scenes.heading: Interests are roots
scenes.narration: An interest is why they want it: a need, a worry, a hope or a fear. Fresh stock for Tuesday clients. Fewer costly machine changeovers. Cash to pay for a new warehouse.

scenes.heading: Ask why, and why not
scenes.narration: To find interests, ask: why does this matter to you? What would happen if you didn't get it? What worries you about our proposal?

scenes.heading: Many keys fit one lock
scenes.narration: Positions usually allow one answer. Interests allow many. Once you know what each side needs, you can design options that satisfy both.

scenes.heading: Fair standards settle the rest
scenes.narration: Where interests do clash, agree on a fair standard, such as market rates, data or an expert view, instead of a battle of wills.

cards.title: The Monday slot: under the surface
cards.caption: Sana and Bilal's positions are opposites. Their interests are not.

items.label: Position
items.left: First production slot every Monday, guaranteed

items.label: Core interest
items.left: Fresh mithai for Tuesday corporate deliveries after an 18-hour truck journey
items.right: Batch similar products to cut machine changeover time and waste

items.label: Fear
items.left: Losing corporate clients to fresher competitors
items.right: Every region demanding a fixed slot and planning collapsing

items.label: Shared interest
items.left: Winning the Eid season for Noor Mithaas
items.right: Winning the Eid season for Noor Mithaas

cards.question: A distributor says, 'We need 60 days' credit, not 30.' Which question is most likely to uncover his interest?
options: 'Would you accept 45 days?'
'Is 60 days your final position?'
'Our other distributors accept 30 days. Why can't you?'
'What happens in your business between day 30 and day 60 that makes the longer period important?'
cards.explanation: Asking why the extra time matters explores the need behind the position, for example when his own retailers pay him. Offering 45 days jumps to a compromise, and the other questions argue about or test the position.

cards.title: Four moves of interest-based negotiation
cards.caption: A widely taught approach from the Harvard Negotiation Project, in our own words.

items.label: Separate people and problem
items.detail: Be soft on the person and firm on the problem. Sit side by side against the issue.

items.label: Focus on interests
items.detail: Look beneath positions for needs, worries and hopes on both sides.

items.label: Invent options for mutual gain
items.detail: Brainstorm several options before judging any, and look for low-cost, high-value trades.

items.label: Use objective criteria
items.detail: Settle remaining differences with fair standards: market rates, data, precedent, expert opinion.

cards.back: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will actually do if this deal fails. It measures your real power at the table.
The least favourable deal you will accept. Worked out from your BATNA: never accept a deal worse than your best alternative.
Zone Of Possible Agreement: the range between the two sides' walk-away points. If they don't overlap, there is no deal on that issue alone.

The first concrete number on the table. It tends to pull the outcome towards it, so open with a credible, justified figure. If they anchor at an extreme, don't bargain from it: re-anchor with a fair standard.

cards.front: Is BATNA the same as your bottom line?
cards.back: No. BATNA is your alternative course of action; your bottom line (walk-away point) is the deal value you derive from it.

cards.front: How do you get more power?
cards.back: Improve your BATNA before you negotiate, and understand theirs. Don't bluff about alternatives you don't have, and don't volunteer that yours is weak.

cards.title: Working the numbers: the distributor
cards.body:
Shahrah Traders sells about **PKR 40 million** of Noor Mithaas products a month. Every **1% of margin = PKR 400,000 a month** (PKR 4.8 million a year).

**Noor Mithaas's BATNA:** appoint a second distributor. Setting up and the sales dip make it costly; Farhana and finance estimate it is only worth switching if Shahrah wants **more than 13%**. So Noor's walk-away point is **13%**.

**Shahrah's BATNA:** a rival brand has offered them **12%**. They would be unlikely to accept less than that from Noor. Their walk-away point is about **12%**.

**ZOPA = 12% to 13%.** Any deal in that range beats both BATNAs. 14% is outside it, so Danish is right not to accept it, but wrong to walk away: a deal is possible.

At **12.5%**, the extra cost is 1.5% x PKR 40m = **PKR 600,000 a month**, half of what 14% would cost (PKR 1.2m).

cards.title: The Shahrah deal at a glance
cards.caption: Numbers you need before you walk into the room.

items.label: Monthly sales via Shahrah
items.detail: So each 1% of margin costs PKR 400,000 a month.

items.label: Shahrah's demand
items.detail: Up from 11%: an extra PKR 1.2m a month. Outside the ZOPA.

items.label: Noor's walk-away point
items.detail: Above this, appointing a second distributor is the better option.

items.label: Zone of possible agreement
items.detail: Between Shahrah's alternative offer (12%) and Noor's walk-away point (13%).

cards.question: If Shahrah's monthly sales stayed at PKR 40 million, how much more a month would a 13% margin cost Noor Mithaas compared with the current 11%?
cards.explanation: 13% minus 11% = 2 percentage points. 2% of PKR 40 million = PKR 800,000 a month. PKR 5.2 million is the full 13% margin, not the increase.

cards.title: Across the table from Shahrah
cards.situation: You meet Shahrah's owner, Mr Khalid, in Karachi. He opens: '14%, or we move to the other brand next week.' In conversation you learn he has just leased a new warehouse in Korangi, his cash flow is tight, and he values Noor Mithaas's Eid demand because it brings retailers into his network. Your walk-away point is 13%.

choices.text: '14% is impossible. Our final offer is 11.5%. Take it or leave it.'
choices.outcome: Mr Khalid walks out, and you have nearly forced both sides into their more expensive alternatives. A hard anchor without exploring interests ignores a ZOPA that clearly exists.

choices.text: 'Let's meet halfway at 12.5%.'
choices.outcome: He accepts, grudgingly. The number is inside the ZOPA, but you've left his cash-flow problem unsolved, and he may come back next season. A reasonable but shallow result.

choices.text: 'Help me understand the cash pressure from Korangi. What if we offered 12.5%, plus 15 extra days' credit during Eid and co-funded shelf displays that pull retailers into your network?'
choices.outcome: Mr Khalid leans in. Extra credit costs Noor little but solves his real problem, and the displays serve both. You settle at 12.5% with seasonal terms, inside the ZOPA and better for both than either alternative. Interests turned a margin fight into a package.

choices.text: 'Fine, 14%. We cannot risk losing Karachi before Eid.'
choices.outcome: You keep Shahrah, but at PKR 400,000 a month more than your own walk-away point. Agreeing to a deal worse than your BATNA is a loss, however relieved you feel.

cards.title: The packaging film quote
cards.body:
Noor Mithaas needs **50,000** printed gift boxes. The current vendor quotes **PKR 95 per box**.

You improve your BATNA before negotiating: a Faisalabad vendor offers **PKR 88 per box**, plus a one-off **PKR 150,000** for new printing plates.

**True cost of the alternative:** PKR 150,000 / 50,000 boxes = PKR 3 per box. 88 + 3 = **PKR 91 per box**.

So your walk-away price with the current vendor is about **PKR 91**, before allowing for the risk of a new supplier during Eid.

You share **objective criteria**: board prices have fallen this quarter, and you show the market index. The vendor agrees to **PKR 91**, matching your alternative without the switching risk. Saving: PKR 4 x 50,000 = **PKR 200,000**.

**Lesson:** work out the full cost of your alternative, including one-off costs, before you set your walk-away price.

cards.title: Now you're the mediator
cards.setting: Farhana's office. The Monday-slot dispute between Sana and Bilal is stuck.

lines.text: The Shahrah deal was excellent. Now the harder one: Sana and Bilal. They've agreed to mediation, and I want you to lead it.
You swallow. You're not their boss, and both are senior to you in years.
That can help. A mediator isn't a judge. Your job is to run a fair process so they find their own agreement.
One warning: you can promise discretion, but not total secrecy. If something like harassment, fraud or a safety risk comes up, it goes to the formal route.
Now, where do you start? Not with both of them in one room.

cards.title: The manager's mediation steps
cards.prompt: Put the mediation steps in the right order.
steps: Meet each person privately: listen, explain the process and check they are willing to take part.
Open the joint meeting: state the purpose, your role as a neutral facilitator and the ground rules.
Let each person tell their view without interruption, then summarise it neutrally.
Build an agenda of issues and turn positions into interests, highlighting common ground.
Generate options together, then test them against interests and fair criteria.
Write down a specific agreement: who does what, by when, and how problems will be raised.
Follow up on an agreed date to check the agreement is working and adjust if needed.

cards.title: Reframe it
cards.prompt: A mediator turns accusations into interests. Match each accusation to the best reframe.

pairs.left: 'He never tells us anything until it's too late.'
pairs.right: 'So you need early warning of changes that affect your plans.'

pairs.left: 'She only cares about her own targets.'
pairs.right: 'So you want your constraints taken into account when sales makes commitments.'

pairs.left: 'The plant treats Karachi like a second-class region.'
pairs.right: 'So fair access to production capacity really matters to you.'
'So you need stable orders after a certain cut-off time.'

pairs.left: 'I'm sick of being the villain in every meeting.'
pairs.right: 'So you want your team's effort recognised, and problems discussed without blame.'

cards.title: Ground rules, caucus and confidentiality
cards.body:
**Ground rules** to agree at the start of a joint meeting:

- one person speaks at a time; no interruptions
- describe behaviour and impact, not character
- what is said stays in the room, **within the limits explained**
- either side, or the mediator, can call a short break

**Your role:** neutral facilitator, not judge. If you have a conflict of interest, for example one party reports to you, say so; consider whether someone else should mediate.

**Caucus:** a private meeting with one party during the mediation. Use it when emotions spike, the talks are stuck or you need to reality-test a position ('What will you do if there's no agreement?'). Meet both sides privately so neither feels excluded, and share what was said only with permission.

**Confidentiality limits:** harassment, discrimination, fraud, safety risks or threats cannot stay inside a mediation. Say this upfront; if it arises, pause and use the formal route.

cards.title: Stuck in the joint meeting
cards.situation: An hour into the mediation, Sana and Bilal have each told their side and you have built an agenda. But on the Monday slot both are repeating their positions, voices are rising and Sana says, 'There's no point in this.' You have not yet held a private session with either during the meeting.

choices.text: Propose a short break and hold a private session with each, asking what they'll do if there's no agreement and which options they could live with.
choices.outcome: In private, Bilal admits long-shelf items could run Mondays without extra changeovers, and Sana admits she only needs the slot for fresh mithai lines. Reality-testing in caucus, with both sides seen privately, breaks the deadlock.
