choices.text: Decide the issue yourself: Karachi gets the slot on alternate Mondays.
choices.outcome: Both now see you as a judge, and neither owns the decision. A mediator who imposes a ruling loses neutrality, and the agreement is weaker for it.

choices.text: End the mediation and report to Farhana that it has failed.
choices.outcome: Rising emotions mid-mediation are normal, not failure. You give up on a process that was close to finding interests both could work with.

choices.text: Remind them of the ground rules and ask them to keep going in the joint meeting.
choices.outcome: Things calm down slightly, but they still repeat their positions. Restating ground rules helps with behaviour, not with deadlock. A caucus would let them explore options without losing face.

cards.title: Negotiation Table cleared
items: Positions are what people demand; interests are why. Ask why and why not, and design options that meet both sides' interests.
Interest-based negotiation: separate people from the problem, focus on interests, invent options for mutual gain, use objective criteria.
Your BATNA sets your walk-away point. Include one-off costs; improve your BATNA before negotiating, and never accept a deal worse than it.
The ZOPA lies between the two walk-away points. A credible, justified anchor and package deals help you land well inside it.
Mediation: private meetings, joint opening and ground rules, uninterrupted stories, interests, options, a specific written agreement and follow-up. Caucus when stuck; know the confidentiality limits.

cards.prompt: Think of a negotiation coming up in your work: with a vendor, client, colleague or your own manager. What is your BATNA, how could you improve it this week, and what interest might sit behind the other side's position?

quiz.question: A plant manager says: 'I won't accept any orders after 4 pm.' Which of the following is most likely his underlying interest?
options: Having enough time to plan materials and shifts for the next day's run
Refusing orders after 4 pm
Winning the argument with the sales team so the plant isn't blamed for late orders
Getting a written policy signed by the CEO
quiz.explanation: 'No orders after 4 pm' is the position. The interest is why he wants it: time to plan materials and shifts. Knowing that opens options, such as a later cut-off for products already in stock.

quiz.question: What does BATNA stand for, and what does it represent?
options: Best Agreement That Negotiators Accept: the final settlement that both sides sign at the end
Basic Acceptable Terms for Negotiation: your opening offer
Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will actually do if this deal fails
Bargaining Advantage Through Negotiated Anchors: the first number you put on the table
quiz.explanation: BATNA is your best alternative course of action if no agreement is reached. It sets your walk-away point and measures your real power at the table.

quiz.question: Your company will pay up to PKR 650,000 a month to rent a warehouse in Lahore. The landlord would accept anything above PKR 600,000. What is the zone of possible agreement?
options: Below PKR 600,000
Above PKR 650,000
There is no ZOPA
quiz.explanation: The ZOPA lies between the landlord's walk-away point (PKR 600,000) and yours (PKR 650,000). Any rent in that range is better for both sides than having no deal.

quiz.question: You need 40,000 units. Your current supplier quotes PKR 128 a unit. An alternative supplier quotes PKR 120 a unit plus a one-off setup charge of PKR 200,000. Ignoring other risks, what is your walk-away price with the current supplier?
options: PKR 120
PKR 122
PKR 125
PKR 128
quiz.explanation: Setup cost per unit: PKR 200,000 / 40,000 = PKR 5. Effective cost of the alternative: 120 + 5 = PKR 125. Paying the current supplier more than PKR 125 would be worse than your BATNA.

quiz.question: Before a tough renegotiation with your only packaging supplier, what is the most effective way to increase your negotiating power?
options: Tell the supplier you have many other options, even though you haven't found any yet
Open with a very aggressive price demand
Ask senior management to call the supplier's owner
Line up and cost a credible alternative supplier to improve your BATNA
quiz.explanation: Power comes from a strong, real alternative. Improving your BATNA before you negotiate changes what you can walk away to. Bluffing about alternatives is risky and can destroy trust if exposed.

quiz.question: A landlord and tenant disagree about how much rent should rise. Which of these is the best example of an objective criterion to settle it?
options: The landlord's statement that he needs more income
The tenant's threat to leave
Whoever has known the property agent longer and therefore understands the market better
Current rents for comparable warehouses in the same area
quiz.explanation: Objective criteria are fair standards independent of either side's will, such as market rates for comparable properties. Needs and threats are each side's own leverage, not neutral standards.

quiz.question: A manager is about to mediate between two supervisors in her department. What should she normally do first?
options: Meet each supervisor privately to listen, explain the process and check willingness
Bring both into a room together and ask who started the dispute, so the facts are clear early
Write a draft agreement for them to sign
Announce the dispute at the team meeting so everyone understands
quiz.explanation: Private preparation lets each person be heard without an audience, builds trust in the process and helps the mediator understand the issues before the joint meeting.

quiz.question: During a mediation, what is the manager's main role?
options: To act as a fair judge who listens carefully to both sides and then decides who is right and why
To act as a neutral facilitator running a fair process so the parties reach their own agreement
To represent the more senior party's interests
To record evidence for a disciplinary hearing
quiz.explanation: A mediator manages the process, not the verdict. Parties are more committed to agreements they build themselves. Taking sides or gathering evidence turns mediation into something else.

quiz.question: In a mediation, when is a caucus (a private meeting with one party) most useful?
options: At the very start, instead of a joint meeting
Only when one party refuses to attend
When talks are stuck or emotions spike, to reality-test positions and explore options privately
At the end, to tell each party privately what the other said, so that both understand each other
quiz.explanation: Caucuses help break deadlock and let people explore options without losing face. What is said privately should be shared only with permission, and both sides should be offered a private session.

quiz.question: Which written outcome of a mediation is the strongest agreement?
options: 'Both parties will communicate better, respect each other's constraints and raise problems early and openly.'
'From 1 March, sales sends changes by 2 pm; the plant confirms by 4 pm; both review on 1 April.'
'Sales will try to avoid late changes where possible.'
'Any future disagreements will be discussed openly.'
quiz.explanation: Good agreements are specific and behavioural: who does what, by when, and when it will be reviewed. Vague promises like 'communicate better' cannot be checked and usually fade.

sessions.title: Culture, Customers, Prevention and the Formal Route
sessions.summary: Bring it all together in the real world: hierarchy, face-saving and family-business dynamics in Pakistani workplaces, conflict across departments and with customers and vendors, preventing conflict with clear roles and agreements, and knowing when a matter must go to HR or a formal grievance.
objectives: Adapt your approach to hierarchy, face-saving, indirect communication and family-business dynamics
Resolve cross-department, customer and vendor conflicts using shared measures, contracts and objective criteria
Prevent conflict with clear roles (RACI), team charters and specific working agreements
Recognise when a conflict must be escalated to HR or a formal grievance, and act correctly when it is

cards.title: The boardroom walk-out
cards.setting: Noor Mithaas boardroom, Lahore. Ten days to Eid. Monthly management meeting.

lines.text: The numbers are clear. Our sugar-free range should launch this Eid, in modern packaging. Traditional boxes are dying.
Forty years this company has sold mithai in the red-and-gold box. Our customers trust that box.
Abbu, with respect, that's sentiment, not strategy. Your view is out of date.
The room goes silent. Haji Aslam stands, picks up his tasbeeh and leaves without a word. Twelve managers stare at the table.
(whispering) In my village, a son doesn't say that to his father in front of the staff.
The Eid Summit is in ten days, and the family is split, a client wants a huge discount and there's something else I need to tell you privately.
This is the final stage: culture, customers, prevention and the formal route. Let's make the truce hold.

scenes.heading: Respect for rank runs deep
scenes.narration: Many Pakistani workplaces are strongly hierarchical. Disagreeing openly with a senior, an elder or an owner can feel disrespectful, so juniors often stay silent or agree in public.

scenes.heading: 'Ji sir' is not always yes
scenes.narration: 'Ji, sir' may mean 'I heard you', not 'I agree' or 'I can do it'. Problems then surface late, when they are expensive.

scenes.heading: Face is precious
scenes.narration: Izzat, a person's standing and dignity, matters enormously. Public criticism or contradiction can feel like a deep humiliation, especially for seniors and elders.

scenes.heading: Disagreement goes indirect
scenes.narration: People may hint, go through a respected intermediary or raise concerns privately. Learn to read these signals. Ask for views before giving your own, and offer written or one-to-one channels to disagree safely.

scenes.heading: Use the culture, don't fight it
scenes.narration: Private conversations, respected go-betweens and solutions that let everyone keep their dignity are powerful tools. Respect and directness can go together.

cards.title: Reading the signals
cards.caption: Before you assume agreement or hostility, check what the behaviour might really mean.

items.label: Agreement
items.left: 'Ji sir, ho jayega' (it will be done)
items.right: 'I heard you', and possibly 'I don't think it's realistic, but I can't say so here'

items.label: Silence
items.right: People disagree but won't contradict the senior person in public

items.label: Go-between
items.left: A colleague raises another's concern for them
items.right: A respectful way to disagree without direct confrontation

items.label: Delay
items.right: Unspoken disagreement or a problem nobody dared report

items.label: Formality
items.left: A usually warm colleague turns stiff and formal
items.right: They feel slighted, often after losing face

cards.question: In a meeting, the GM asks whether the new delivery plan is workable. Every supervisor says 'Ji sir'. What is the best next step?
options: Follow up one-to-one or in writing, asking each supervisor what could go wrong and what they would need
Treat it as full agreement and launch the plan
Criticise the supervisors for not speaking up
Repeat the question louder in the meeting
cards.explanation: In hierarchical settings, public agreement may only mean 'I heard you'. Private or written follow-up, framed around risks and needs, gives people a face-safe way to raise doubts before they become expensive.

cards.title: Family-business dynamics
cards.body:
In a family business, people often wear several hats at once: **family member, owner and manager**. A well-known model shows these as three overlapping circles. Conflict flares where they overlap:

- a father-son disagreement about strategy becomes a family rift
- family members get roles or pay professionals see as unfair
- professional managers don't know whose instruction to follow
- succession is unspoken, so every disagreement is really about who will lead next

**Tools that help:**

- a **family council** that meets separately from management meetings
- a written **family charter (constitution)** on roles, employment of family members and how disputes are resolved
- clear **decision rights** for family and professional managers
- a board with **independent members** or a respected outside advisor
- disagreements between elders and juniors handled **in private**, often through a trusted intermediary

cards.title: After the walk-out
cards.situation: Haji Aslam hasn't spoken to Danish for two days. Danish insists the sugar-free decision can't wait. Farhana asks how you would help, as a non-family manager. You know Aslam respects Farhana, and that the sugar-free range has strong test results but no customer data yet for the traditional market.

choices.text: Tell Danish to apologise publicly at the next management meeting so the staff see the issue closed.
choices.outcome: A public apology humiliates Danish in turn and puts the family's quarrel on show again. Face matters to both, so repair is best done privately.

choices.text: Suggest Farhana meets Haji sahib privately first; then a private family meeting where Danish acknowledges the hurt and proposes a limited Eid pilot in the red-and-gold box with a sugar-free label.
choices.outcome: Aslam's dignity is restored in private, through a respected intermediary. The pilot builds on his legacy rather than rejecting it, and gives Danish real data. Both can say yes without losing face.

choices.text: Stay out of it. Family matters are not for professional managers.
choices.outcome: The silence spreads: managers get conflicting instructions from father and son, and the Eid range is stuck. Avoiding the family side is wise; avoiding the business impact is not.

choices.text: Write a neutral memo to both with the data and let them decide.
choices.outcome: The data helps, but a memo can't repair the hurt from a public contradiction. The relationship and face issue has to be addressed first, or the data will be read as taking sides.

cards.title: What Farhana couldn't say in the corridor

lines.text: Two things. First, the corporate client wants a 20% discount on the whole gift-box order for the late delivery.
(on speaker) They're threatening to post about us on LinkedIn. Should I just give them what they want?
Second, and this stays between us: a packer on the night shift has complained that a line supervisor keeps making comments about her appearance and asked for her number.
(called in) That supervisor is one of my best. Let me sit them both down and sort it out quietly. No need for HR drama before Eid.
No, Bilal. Some conflicts are not ours to mediate. This one goes to the formal route, and today.

cards.title: Resolve informally or escalate?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation: can a manager handle it informally, or must it go to HR or a formal process?
buckets: Escalate to HR or formal route

items.text: Two packers argue about who gets the seat near the fan
A supervisor repeatedly comments on a worker's appearance and asks for her number
Sales and dispatch disagree about cut-off times for orders
An employee says a colleague threatened to 'deal with him' outside the gate
A team member feels left out of client meetings
A worker reports that a manager is changing weighbridge records
A manager repeatedly mocks an employee's religious sect in front of others
Two analysts clash over the format of the monthly report

cards.title: When it must leave your desk
cards.body:
Informal resolution is the right first step for most disagreements, **but not all**. Escalate to HR or the formal process when there is:

- **harassment**, including sexual harassment, or **discrimination** (for example by gender, religion, sect, ethnicity or disability)
- **violence, threats** or safety risks
- **fraud, theft or ethical breaches**, which often belong in a whistleblowing channel
- **serious misconduct** or a possible legal claim
- a big **power imbalance** that makes informal talks unfair
- a **pattern** that continues after informal attempts, or a party asking for the formal route

Pakistan's workplace harassment law (the 2010 Act, as amended, plus provincial versions) requires employers to have an **inquiry committee** and a **code of conduct**, and lets complainants also approach an **Ombudsperson**. Rules on scope and procedure have changed over time, so check the current federal or provincial law and your own policy.

**Don't** investigate yourself, pressure the complainant to 'settle quietly' or tip off the accused.

cards.title: The formal route, done fairly
cards.caption: Exact steps and time limits depend on your policy and the law that applies to your workers. The principles are constant.

items.label: Receive and record
items.detail: Take the complaint seriously, record it accurately and acknowledge it in writing.

items.label: Protect
items.detail: Interim measures if needed, such as shift changes that don't penalise the complainant. Make clear that retaliation is forbidden.

items.label: Investigate impartially
items.detail: An unbiased person or committee gathers evidence and statements. Confidentiality on a need-to-know basis.

items.label: Hear both sides
items.detail: The person accused is told the allegations and gets a fair chance to respond.

items.label: Decide and document
items.detail: A reasoned decision proportionate to the findings, communicated to both parties.

items.label: Appeal and follow up
items.detail: A route to appeal, and checks that the working environment is safe afterwards.

cards.back: The person or people who do the work. There can be several.
The one person who owns the outcome and has the final say. Only one A per activity, or conflict follows.
People whose input is sought before the decision. Two-way conversation.
People who are told after the decision. One-way communication.
A short written agreement on how a team works: how it decides, communicates, handles disagreement and how fast members respond.
Specific promises such as cut-off times, turnaround times and an escalation path, ideally with a shared measure both sides own.

cards.title: Which tool prevents which fight?
cards.prompt: Match each prevention tool to the recurring conflict it would most directly prevent.

pairs.right: Sales, finance and the plant all think they approve rush orders.
Sales is rewarded for volume and the plant for cost, so each blames the other for late orders.
Orders keep changing at 6 pm for next-morning production.
Problems are fought out in the WhatsApp group instead of a proper forum.
Professional managers get conflicting instructions from the founder and his son.

cards.title: The client's discount demand
cards.caption: Objective criteria: what the signed purchase order actually says about late delivery.

items.label: Client's demand
items.detail: Off the whole PKR 6.4m order (8,000 boxes x PKR 800) = PKR 1.28m.

items.label: Late consignment
items.detail: 5,200 boxes x PKR 800, delivered 3 days late. The 2,800 undelivered boxes are not invoiced.

items.label: Contract penalty
items.detail: Of the late consignment's value, capped at 10%.

items.label: Penalty due
items.detail: 3 days x 2% = 6% of PKR 4.16m. Well below the cap and the demand.

cards.question: If the 5,200 boxes had arrived 6 days late instead of 3, what would the contract penalty be?
cards.explanation: 6 days x 2% = 12%, but the penalty is capped at 10%. 10% of PKR 4.16 million = PKR 416,000. PKR 499,200 forgets the cap.

cards.title: The LinkedIn threat
cards.situation: The client's procurement head emails: '20% off the whole order, or we post about Noor Mithaas's failure on LinkedIn and move our Eid business elsewhere next year.' The contract penalty is PKR 249,600; the demand is PKR 1.28 million. The client spends about PKR 15 million a year with you, and you learn their own CEO was embarrassed when gift boxes reached his top clients late.

choices.text: Pay the 20% to avoid the post. Reputation matters more than PKR 1 million.
choices.outcome: The client takes the money and learns that threats work. Next year's negotiation starts with another threat. Accommodating a demand far outside fair criteria rewards the tactic.

choices.text: Reply that the contract allows 6% of the late consignment and nothing more, and that threats are unprofessional.
choices.outcome: You are right on the numbers, but the client feels lectured and the relationship cools. Objective criteria work best alongside the client's real interests, not instead of them.

choices.text: Call the procurement head, acknowledge the embarrassment, apply the contract penalty in full and offer a goodwill package for their CEO's clients, such as priority Eid slots and personalised replacement boxes.
choices.outcome: The client hears an apology and a fair, contract-based penalty, plus something that fixes their real problem: face with their own VIPs. The post never happens and next year's order is secured.

cards.title: A truce kit for departments, customers and vendors
cards.body:
**Between departments**
- one shared measure both sides own (such as on-time-in-full delivery)
- a written service agreement: cut-offs, turnaround times, who to call
- a short weekly interface meeting for problems, not the WhatsApp group

**With customers and vendors**
- put specs, delivery terms, penalties and change procedures in the contract
- include a dispute clause: talk first, then mediation, then arbitration or court
- confirm verbal changes in writing, even by WhatsApp or email
- if a complaint goes public, acknowledge it briefly in public, then move the conversation private
- separate the person from the problem: be warm to the person and firm on the terms

cards.title: The Eid Summit
cards.body:
Ten days later, the whole leadership team meets.

- **Family:** after Farhana's private meeting with Haji Aslam and a family-only dinner, Danish presents a sugar-free pilot **in the red-and-gold box**. Haji sahib announces it himself. A family council will meet quarterly from now on.
- **Plant and sales:** the mediated agreement is signed. Fresh lines get the Monday slot, order changes close at 2 pm, and both teams share an on-time-in-full target.
- **Roles:** a RACI chart names you as the one Accountable for rush-order approval, with the plant Consulted on capacity.
- **Shahrah Traders:** 12.5% margin with seasonal credit, inside the ZOPA.
- **The client:** penalty paid per contract, goodwill package delivered, next year's order confirmed.
- **The complaint:** handled by the inquiry committee, with the night shift reorganised so the complainant isn't disadvantaged.

Farhana raises her chai: 'You didn't remove conflict. You made it useful.'

cards.title: The truce holds
items: In hierarchical cultures, 'ji sir' may not mean agreement: create private and written channels, and protect face by correcting in private.
Family businesses need clear roles, a family council or charter and private handling of disputes between elders and juniors.
Prevent conflict with one Accountable per activity (RACI), team charters, shared measures and specific working agreements.
With customers and vendors, combine empathy for their interests with objective criteria such as the contract.
Harassment, discrimination, threats, fraud and serious misconduct go to the formal route: record, protect, investigate impartially, hear both sides, decide, allow appeal and never retaliate.

cards.prompt: Pick one recurring conflict in your organisation. Which prevention tool (RACI, a team charter, a shared measure or a working agreement) would stop it coming back, and who would you need to involve to put it in place?

quiz.question: In a strongly hierarchical team, a junior officer says 'Ji sir, ho jayega' when given a deadline that looks impossible. What is the safest interpretation?
options: He may just be acknowledging it; check privately what he'd need to meet it
He fully agrees and is confident he can deliver
He is being deliberately dishonest
He is challenging your authority indirectly by agreeing to something he knows can't be done
quiz.explanation: In high-hierarchy settings, public agreement may mean 'I heard you' rather than 'I can do it'. A private, face-safe check surfaces risks early without accusing anyone.

quiz.question: During a presentation to clients, your senior director quotes an outdated price. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Correct him immediately in front of the clients
Say nothing at all, since he is senior
Pass him a discreet note or raise it during a break so he can correct it himself
Email the clients afterwards with the correct price, so he isn't embarrassed in the room
quiz.explanation: The error must be fixed, but in a way that protects his face: privately, letting him make the correction himself. Public correction humiliates him; silence or going around him creates bigger problems.

quiz.question: Professional managers in a family business keep receiving conflicting instructions from the founder and his daughter. Which tool most directly addresses the root cause?
options: A team-building retreat for all managers, the founder and his daughter together
A larger bonus for managers to compensate for the confusion
Asking managers to follow whoever spoke to them last
A family charter and clear decision rights setting out who decides what
quiz.explanation: The root cause is overlapping family, ownership and management roles without clear decision rights. A family charter, often with a family council, sets out who decides what.

quiz.question: In a RACI chart for approving rush orders, both the sales head and the finance head are marked 'A'. What is the likely problem?
options: With two people owning the final say, disputes over the decision are likely
Nobody will do the work
Too many people will be informed
Nothing; shared accountability between sales and finance is good governance practice
quiz.explanation: RACI works only with one Accountable person per activity. Two A's means two final decision-makers, a recipe for process conflict. Others can be Consulted or Responsible instead.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a team charter?
options: To list each team member's salary and grade
To record disciplinary warnings
To replace the company's HR policies with rules the team members have chosen for themselves
To agree in writing how the team decides, communicates, disagrees and responds
quiz.explanation: A team charter sets shared working norms up front, so many process and relationship conflicts never start. It sits alongside HR policy, not instead of it.

quiz.question: Credit control keeps blocking orders from slow-paying customers, and sales keeps escalating to the CEO to release them. Which measure would most help prevent this recurring conflict?
options: Letting sales override credit holds whenever a customer is important to the company's growth
A shared target, such as collected (not booked) sales, plus an agreed rule for holds
Moving credit control to report to the sales head
Asking the CEO to decide each case personally
quiz.explanation: Both teams succeed only when sales are booked and collected, so a shared measure aligns them, and an agreed rule removes ad-hoc escalation. Giving one side power over the other just moves the conflict.

quiz.question: A worker tells her manager that a colleague keeps sending her messages of a sexual nature. The manager offers to 'sit you both down and sort it out'. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing; informal resolution is always the best first step, and it avoids embarrassing anyone
The manager should have waited until the worker complained twice
Harassment belongs in the formal route, such as the inquiry committee, not in mediation
The manager should only act if there are witnesses
quiz.explanation: Harassment involves a power and safety issue and is covered by specific law and policy. Mediating it as an ordinary dispute can pressure the complainant and breach the organisation's duties. It goes to the formal process.

quiz.question: Which principle is essential in a fair formal grievance process?
options: The complainant's line manager always investigates
The accused hears the allegations and can respond, and retaliation is forbidden
Details are shared with the whole team so everyone understands
Decisions are made quickly and without much documentation, to limit the company's legal risk
quiz.explanation: Fairness requires hearing both sides and protecting the complainant from retaliation. Investigations should be impartial, confidential on a need-to-know basis and well documented.

quiz.question: A contract sets a late-delivery penalty of 2% of the late consignment's value per day, capped at 10%. A PKR 2,000,000 consignment arrives 4 days late. What penalty is due?
quiz.explanation: 4 days x 2% = 8%, which is under the 10% cap. 8% of PKR 2,000,000 = PKR 160,000. PKR 200,000 would apply only at the cap.

quiz.question: A supply contract includes a dispute-resolution clause. Which sequence is the most typical and sensible?
options: Court first, then negotiation if the court is slow
Arbitration first, then mediation
Direct negotiation, then mediation, then arbitration or court
A public complaint on social media first, then negotiation once the other side is under pressure
quiz.explanation: Clauses usually escalate from the cheapest, most relationship-friendly step (talking) through mediation to a binding decision by an arbitrator or court. Starting with litigation is costly and damages the relationship.

bank.question: At a telecom company, the IT service desk complains that HR 'sits on new-joiner access forms to show its power'. HR says IT 'sends half-complete requests'. Neither team's procedure says which details a request must include or how fast it should be processed. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: A relationship conflict between the two team heads that needs an off-site team-building retreat
A task conflict about which systems new joiners should be given access to
A values conflict about honesty that senior management must investigate
A process conflict rooted in an undefined procedure, now being misattributed to motives
bank.explanation: The underlying issue is an undefined process (what details, what turnaround). Each side explains delays by the other's motives, which is misattribution. Team-building alone treats the symptom; defining the procedure removes the root.

bank.question: Two regional managers in a pharma company are in dispute over territory boundaries. Both now copy the national sales director on every email, each has persuaded his team that the other region is 'stealing' doctors, and they have stopped sharing market data. What does the stage of escalation suggest you do?
options: Act as a third party: meet each privately, then run a structured joint meeting on the boundaries
Encourage them to have a direct conversation, since experienced managers can still resolve it themselves
Ignore it until targets close, because the dispute is about business, not people
Immediately start formal disciplinary proceedings against both
bank.explanation: Recruiting allies, copying bosses and withholding information are stage 4 signs. At that level the parties rarely self-resolve, so a third party is needed, starting privately. Nothing yet shows the threats or sabotage that might justify formal action.

bank.question: A bank's operations head says: 'My team is always arguing about how to redesign the account-opening process. I want to ban debate and just tell them the answer.' The arguments are heated but focused on the process steps, and the team still socialises together. What is the best advice?
options: Agree with him, because any open conflict eventually turns personal and will damage the team's results over time
Keep the debate, structured around evidence and a clear decision rule; this is task conflict with trust
Separate the people who disagree most so they cannot argue
Ask HR to run a conflict-style assessment before any further meetings
bank.explanation: Debate about the work in a team with good relationships is functional and can improve the design. Banning it loses ideas and buy-in. The leader's job is to keep it about evidence and to make it clear how and when the decision will be made.

bank.question: A quality manager refuses to sign off a batch certificate that 'rounds up' a test result, saying it would be dishonest. The production head says it is a tiny variance and that missing the shipment will cost a major customer. Which approach best fits the nature of this conflict?
options: Split the difference: sign the certificate, but record the true result in the internal quality file
Let the more senior manager decide, since this is a task conflict
Treat it as a relationship problem and ask the two managers to apologise to each other
Treat it as a values issue: don't press for dishonesty; look at retesting or telling the customer
bank.explanation: Integrity is a values issue, and here it also has regulatory and safety implications. Bargaining away honesty is not acceptable. The productive route is to search for options that respect the boundary, such as retesting, an honest customer conversation or a partial shipment.

bank.question: Noor Mithaas estimates that 5 managers spent 4 hours a week for 6 weeks on a dispute, at PKR 3,000 an hour, and that the dispute cost a PKR 180,000 penalty discount from a client. What is the total measurable cost?
bank.explanation: Time: 5 x 4 = 20 hours a week; 20 x 6 weeks = 120 hours; 120 x PKR 3,000 = PKR 360,000. Add the PKR 180,000 penalty: PKR 540,000. PKR 360,000 counts the time only.

bank.question: Ahmed, a senior accountant, has been quietly resentful for months because his colleague Kiran is given all the visible projects. Kiran has no idea. Ahmed has started sending her information late. How should a manager view this?
options: It is a conflict: one party perceives his goals as blocked, and it is already changing behaviour
It is not a conflict, because Kiran does not know about it
It is purely a performance issue with Ahmed's timeliness, to be handled firmly in his next performance appraisal
It is a values conflict about fairness that cannot be addressed
bank.explanation: Conflict lives in perception. One party who feels blocked and changes behaviour has started a conflict, even if the other side is unaware. Treating it only as a timeliness issue misses the cause the manager needs to address.

bank.question: Which change in language most clearly signals that a dispute has moved from hardening to personalising?
options: From 'I think we should do X' to 'I am completely sure that X is the only right answer for this company'
From 'your proposal ignores cost' to 'you always ignore cost because you only care about your targets'
From discussing the issue in a meeting to discussing it by email
From disagreeing politely to disagreeing firmly
bank.explanation: Personalising means the other person and their motives become the problem: generalisations ('always') and assumed motives. Firmer certainty or a change of channel can happen at hardening without the dispute turning personal.

bank.question: A retail chain's store managers clash with the central merchandising team, saying the team 'doesn't care about stores'. On inspection, merchandising is measured on stock turnover and stores on full shelves and sales. What is the most durable fix?
options: Add a shared measure, such as on-shelf availability within stock targets, so both succeed together
Run regular listening sessions where store managers can share their frustrations directly with the merchandising team
Replace the head of merchandising with someone more cooperative
Tell store managers to escalate every disagreement to the regional director
bank.explanation: The root is structural: KPIs pull in opposite directions. A shared measure aligns incentives so the disputes stop recurring. Replacing people or venting sessions leave the structure that generates conflict in place.

bank.question: Two engineers in a power company dispute a maintenance schedule. One has started delaying the other's work permits even though it risks a penalty for the company, saying 'if I lose, he loses more'. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask them to work out a compromise between themselves
Facilitate a joint brainstorming session so that both engineers can design the new schedule options together
Wait to see whether the penalty teaches them a lesson
Senior intervention: separate their decisions, protect operations and start a formal HR process
bank.explanation: Accepting harm to oneself and the company to hurt the other is the lose-lose phase (stage 5). Facilitation alone is rarely enough at this point; operations must be protected and the behaviour handled through senior and formal routes.

bank.question: A customer-service team in Islamabad has constant friction: agents accuse each other of 'dumping' difficult calls. The team lead plans a personality workshop. You find that no rule says who owns a call once it is transferred. What should come first?
options: Run the personality workshop first, so that relationships are repaired before anything else changes
A clear call-ownership rule agreed with the team, then a check on whether the friction remains
A disciplinary warning for the agents who complain most
Moving the most vocal agents to a different shift
bank.explanation: The friction has a process root: unclear ownership after transfer. Fix the process first; much of the 'personality' conflict may disappear. If relationship damage remains, then work on it. Discipline or reshuffles ignore the cause.

bank.question: A quality test at a dairy plant shows a batch may be contaminated. The sales director objects to holding it, as a major retailer's promotion starts tomorrow. The plant head must decide in the next hour. Which response best reflects good conflict-mode choice?
options: Compete: hold the batch now, explain to sales, then work together on supplying the retailer
Collaborate with sales on a solution that meets both concerns before deciding anything at all
Compromise: release half the batch to the retailer and hold the rest
Accommodate sales to protect the retailer relationship, then test again later
bank.explanation: Food safety is a non-negotiable line and time is short, so a firm competing decision is right. Collaboration can follow on how to supply the retailer. Releasing half splits a safety principle, which is never acceptable.

bank.question: Your company is redesigning credit terms with a distributor it has worked with for 12 years. Both sides have data and ideas, the new terms will run for three years, and the deadline is a month away. The distributor's first position is 'we need 60 days' credit'. Which approach is most likely to produce the best outcome?
options: Compromise quickly at 45 days to protect the relationship
Accommodate the 60 days to show goodwill
Compete: insist on the current 30 days, because you have the stronger brand and they need you
Collaborate: explore why they need 60 days and design terms that meet both sides' real needs
bank.explanation: High stakes, a long relationship, time available and the need for both sides to live with the terms all favour collaborating. Exploring the reason behind 60 days may reveal options, such as payment linked to their sell-out cycle, that beat a split at 45.

bank.question: Two department heads of equal rank have spent two meetings trying to find a joint solution for sharing a PKR 5 million IT budget, but their needs are genuinely exclusive. The budget must be submitted tomorrow. What is the most sensible next step?
options: Keep collaborating until a solution that fully satisfies both is found, even if the deadline is missed
Both heads should avoid the issue and let finance decide
Agree a fair compromise split for this year and plan a joint review of priorities next quarter
The head with the more urgent project should compete and take the full amount
bank.explanation: Compromise is a sensible fallback when collaboration has been tried and failed, power is equal and time is short. A temporary settlement with a later review preserves the relationship. Missing the deadline or letting finance decide by default helps nobody.

bank.question: A newly appointed manager insists on long consensus meetings for every decision, including the office snack menu and the colour of new files. Important decisions are delayed and the team is frustrated. What is the best feedback?
options: She should switch to competing on every decision to save time
She is overusing compromising; she should push harder for her own view
She is overusing collaborating; save it for important issues and decide small ones quickly
She is using the right mode; the team simply needs more patience while they learn to work together
bank.explanation: Collaborating on trivial matters wastes time and energy, a classic overuse cost. The fix is to match the mode to the stakes, not to swing to competing on everything.

bank.question: You are negotiating a large annual contract with a corporate client next month. This week the client asks you to waive a PKR 15,000 delivery charge on a small order, which matters much more to their procurement officer than to you. What is the best mode for this request?
options: Competing, to show that you will not give anything away before the big annual negotiation starts
Avoiding, by not replying until after the annual contract is signed
Compromising, by offering to waive half the charge
Accommodating, waiving the charge to build goodwill ahead of the bigger negotiation
bank.explanation: When an issue matters little to you but a lot to the other side, and goodwill has future value, accommodating is a smart choice. Haggling over half the charge spends goodwill for little gain.

bank.question: Two vendors who supply another department are in a dispute with each other, and their department head is already managing it. One vendor calls you, as a manager in a different department, asking you to intervene. What is the most appropriate mode?
options: Collaborating, by setting up a meeting with both vendors
Avoiding, by politely declining and directing the vendor to the department head who is handling it
Competing, by telling the vendor he is wrong
Accommodating, by agreeing to raise the vendor's concerns with senior management in your department this week
bank.explanation: Avoiding is appropriate when someone else is better placed to resolve the issue. Stepping in would undermine the responsible manager and confuse the vendors. Referring the vendor on is constructive avoiding.

bank.question: An engineering team and a procurement team disagree about a safety-valve specification. Engineering requires a pressure rating of 40 bar; procurement wants a cheaper 30-bar valve. A manager suggests settling on 35 bar. What is the main flaw?
options: A safety requirement shouldn't be split; the real question is whether 40 bar is truly needed
Compromising is too slow for this kind of decision, so the manager should simply decide it alone and move on
Compromising always damages relationships
The manager should have avoided the issue
bank.explanation: Compromise suits divisible issues of moderate importance, not safety thresholds or principles. A valve rated between the two values may simply be unsafe. The right route is to test the requirement with evidence, then decide firmly.

bank.question: Which of these responses shows avoiding being used constructively rather than harmfully?
options: 'I need the sales data to judge this fairly. I'll have it Thursday; let's meet Friday at 10.'
'Let's not talk about the bonus allocation; it always causes trouble.'
'This isn't really my problem, so I'll let you two work it out somehow.'
'Let's wait and see whether it resolves itself over the next few months; these things often settle down.'
bank.explanation: Constructive avoiding is temporary, has a reason (here, gathering facts) and sets a clear time to return. The others leave the issue unaddressed with no plan, which is how conflicts fester.

bank.question: During a dispute about a shared delivery van, the Lahore manager says: 'You have it Monday to Wednesday, we'll take it Thursday to Saturday.' The Karachi manager replies: 'Before we split it, can you tell me what your Thursday loads look like? Maybe one route can cover both.' Which modes are being used, in order?
options: Collaborating, then compromising
Compromising, then collaborating
Accommodating, then competing
Competing, then avoiding
bank.explanation: Splitting the week is compromising, each side getting part. Asking about the underlying loads to find a solution that serves both fully is collaborating.

bank.question: A senior manager tells a junior finance officer to post a large expense into the next quarter so this quarter's results look better. The officer believes this would misstate the accounts. Which approach best fits?
options: Accommodating, because the manager is senior and carries responsibility for the accounting decision
Compromising, by posting half the expense in each quarter
Avoiding, by delaying the posting and hoping the manager forgets
Compete on the principle: decline politely but firmly, and escalate properly if pressed
bank.explanation: Misstating accounts crosses an ethical and legal line, which is a non-negotiable. Firmly declining is competing on principle, best done respectfully and backed by the proper escalation route. Splitting the expense is still a misstatement.

bank.question: At 11 pm a colleague posts in the team WhatsApp group: 'Some people here clearly don't read emails before making promises to clients.' You know it's aimed at you, and you're furious. What is the best response?
options: Reply immediately in the group with the full email trail, proving that you were right all along
Leave the group so you don't have to see the messages
Don't reply tonight; tomorrow, once calm, call the colleague privately and propose a meeting
Reply with a short, polite but pointed message so the group knows your side
bank.explanation: Replying while hot, especially in public, escalates and creates a permanent record. Moving the issue to a private, calm conversation addresses it without a public face battle. Leaving the group is avoidance that leaves the issue standing.

bank.question: In a budget review, the CFO criticises your forecast in front of your peers. You feel your heart racing and an urge to interrupt. Which response best applies self-regulation?
options: Interrupt at once to defend your numbers before the criticism spreads to the others in the room
Stay completely silent for the rest of the meeting to avoid conflict
Breathe slowly, silently name the feeling, then ask which assumption concerns him
Agree with all the criticism to end the discomfort quickly
bank.explanation: Breathing and naming the emotion bring the thinking brain back; a clarifying question turns a threat into information. Interrupting acts on the alarm, silence withdraws, and agreeing with everything abandons a forecast that may be sound.

bank.question: A factory worker arrives at the HR counter shouting that his overtime has been underpaid for two months. Other employees are queuing. What should the HR officer do first?
options: Invite him to a private room, sit down and let him explain fully before checking any figures
Explain the overtime calculation rules clearly so he understands exactly where he went wrong in his claim
Ask security to remove him because he is disturbing others
Tell him to submit a written complaint and come back next week
bank.explanation: The funnel starts with safety, privacy and listening. Explaining rules before he feels heard sends him back up the heat, removing him escalates without cause, and deferring for a week ignores a possibly genuine pay problem.

bank.question: A team member says angrily: 'I worked all weekend on the presentation and Danish didn't even mention my name to the board.' Which acknowledgement is the strongest?
options: 'I'm sure he just forgot in the pressure of the board meeting. Please don't take it personally; he values you.'
'That happens to everyone; it's part of corporate life.'
'You should raise this directly with Danish if it bothers you.'
'You gave up your weekend and got no recognition from the board. It sounds like your effort felt invisible.'
bank.explanation: A strong acknowledgement reflects both the facts (weekend work, no mention) and the emotion (feeling invisible). Reassurance and normalising dismiss the feeling, and jumping to advice skips acknowledgement.

bank.question: During a dispute about a warning letter, an employee stands up, clenches his fists and says, 'You'll regret this when you leave the building tonight.' What is the right response?
options: Acknowledge his feelings and continue the meeting calmly so the dispute is resolved today
End the meeting, move to safety, alert security or colleagues and report the threat
Set a boundary and offer to continue after a fifteen-minute break
Ignore the comment as a heat-of-the-moment remark
bank.explanation: A threat of violence moves the matter out of de-escalation and mediation into safety and disciplinary processes. Safety comes first: don't stay alone with the person, get help and report it. A boundary-and-break approach suits shouting, not threats.

bank.question: You must speak to Hira, a team lead whose team keeps missing handover deadlines. Which opening best combines a third story with a clear purpose?
options: 'Hira, I think we see the handover deadlines differently. I'd like to understand your side and agree a plan for both teams.'
'Hira, your team's deadlines have become a real problem, and I need it fixed.'
'Hira, I don't want to make a big deal of this at all, but a few people have been complaining about your team's handovers lately.'
'Hira, how are things going in general? Anything bothering you?'
bank.explanation: It names the issue honestly, treats both views as valid and sets a shared purpose. The alternatives either accuse, hide vaguely behind other people's complaints, or avoid the topic altogether, which can feel like a trap when the real issue finally arrives.

bank.question: A project failed because the IT team delivered late and the business team changed the requirements three times. In the review, the business head says, 'IT is entirely to blame.' What would a manager using contribution mapping do?
options: Agree that IT is to blame because they missed the deadline
Escalate the matter to the CEO so that a clear decision on accountability can be made by someone senior
Declare that nobody is to blame so the meeting stays positive
Ask each team, starting with the business side, what they did that contributed and would change
bank.explanation: Contribution mapping looks at what each party did to create the outcome, including the complaining side's three requirement changes, so that both can change. It does not mean nobody is accountable, and escalating for a verdict keeps everyone in blame mode.

bank.question: A supervisor drafts this feedback: 'In yesterday's audit meeting, you were disrespectful to the auditor, which made us look bad.' Which part should be rewritten to fit the Situation-Behaviour-Impact model?
options: 'In yesterday's audit meeting', because the situation is too specific
'You were disrespectful', because it is a judgement, not an observable behaviour
'Which made us look bad', because impact should never be mentioned in feedback to a colleague
Nothing; it already follows the model
bank.explanation: 'Disrespectful' is a label the person can argue with. The behaviour should be something you could film, for example 'you interrupted the auditor twice and said the question was pointless'. The situation is rightly specific, and impact is a core part of the model.

bank.question: A respected senior engineer becomes defensive when told that his design review missed a defect: 'Twenty years I've done this, and now I'm being treated like a trainee.' What is the most effective next move?
options: Repeat the facts of the defect more firmly and in more detail, so that the point finally lands with him
Drop the feedback to protect the relationship
Clarify what you are and aren't saying: you value his expertise; this is one step, one defect
Bring his line manager into the meeting to support your point
bank.explanation: His reaction comes from the identity layer: he hears a judgement on his competence. Clarifying the limited scope of the feedback while affirming his expertise addresses the identity threat without dropping the issue. Repeating the facts harder ignores what is driving the reaction.

bank.question: Two managers had a shouting match in a meeting. After two minutes, one says, 'Okay, I'm fine now, let's finish the decision.' Both still look tense and flushed. What does the science of the threat response suggest?
options: Continue, since they have both agreed to carry on
Ask each manager to apologise to the other before the decision is made, so the tone is reset properly
Take a longer break, often 20 minutes or more, because the body cools slower than it heats
Let the more senior manager make the decision immediately
bank.explanation: Physical arousal falls more slowly than it rises, so a two-minute pause usually isn't enough for clear thinking. A meaningful break or a later session gives the decision a better chance. Apologies or senior decisions don't address the physical state.

bank.question: A retailer will not pay more than 9% above the current price for your product. You cannot supply at less than 10% above it without losing money. What does this mean, and what is the best next step?
options: The ZOPA is 9-10%, so settle at 9.5%
Accept 9% to keep the relationship, because a small loss on this order is better than having no deal
There is a ZOPA because both sides want a deal; split the difference
No ZOPA on price alone; explore other terms such as volume or payment timing, or use your BATNA
bank.explanation: The retailer's maximum (9%) is below your minimum (10%), so no price-only deal beats both alternatives. Adding other issues can create a ZOPA through trades; otherwise you go to your BATNA. Accepting below your walk-away point is a loss.

bank.question: A distributor sells PKR 25 million of your products a month and asks to raise his margin from 10% to 12%. What would the increase cost your company over a full year?
bank.explanation: 2 percentage points of PKR 25 million = PKR 500,000 a month. Over 12 months that's PKR 6,000,000. PKR 36 million would be the whole 12% margin for a year.

bank.question: You buy 100,000 kg of sugar a season. Your current supplier quotes PKR 222 a kg. An alternative quotes PKR 210 a kg, but you would pay PKR 6 a kg more in transport and a one-off PKR 300,000 for quality testing. Ignoring other risks, what is your walk-away price with the current supplier?
options: PKR 210 a kg
PKR 216 a kg
PKR 219 a kg
PKR 222 a kg
bank.explanation: One-off cost per kg: 300,000 / 100,000 = PKR 3. Alternative's true cost: 210 + 6 + 3 = PKR 219. Above PKR 219 the alternative is better; PKR 216 forgets the testing cost.

bank.question: You are renegotiating with a software vendor. You have not yet found any alternative vendor, and the contract expires in three weeks. The vendor's account manager asks, 'Are you talking to anyone else?' What is the wisest approach?
options: Say that you have three other offers that are much cheaper, so the vendor feels real pressure to cut its price
Keep your weak position private, focus on interests and fair criteria, and urgently build an alternative
Admit you have no alternative so the vendor will trust you
Refuse to continue until the vendor reveals its own alternatives
bank.explanation: You need not reveal a weak BATNA, and lying about offers risks your credibility. Focusing on interests and fair criteria keeps talks productive, while working on an alternative strengthens your real position.

bank.question: A landlord opens a rent negotiation at PKR 900,000 a month for a property where comparable rents are around PKR 650,000. What is the best response?
options: Don't counter near his anchor; cite comparable rents as a fair standard and make a justified offer
Counter at PKR 800,000 to show you are reasonable and willing to meet him somewhere close to the halfway point
Accept quickly before he raises it further
Counter at PKR 400,000 to balance his extreme number
bank.explanation: An extreme anchor pulls outcomes towards it if you bargain from it. Re-anchoring with a fair, objective standard resets the discussion. An equally extreme counter-anchor damages credibility and the relationship.

bank.question: In a mediation, a dispatch supervisor says, 'The warehouse team are lazy. They never have pallets ready when my trucks arrive.' Which response by the mediator is the best reframe?
options: 'Let's not call people lazy, please. In this room we describe behaviour, not character.'
'So the warehouse team is the problem here.'
'Can you prove they are lazy? Please give me specific dates and examples so we can check.'
'So it really matters to you that pallets are ready when the trucks arrive.'
bank.explanation: A good reframe drops the accusation and keeps the underlying interest, which both sides can work on. Correcting the language alone misses the need, agreeing with the label takes sides, and demanding proof turns mediation into a trial.

bank.question: A branch manager opens a mediation between two tellers by saying, 'I've reviewed everything and I think Ayesha is mostly right, but let's hear from both of you.' What is the main problem?
options: She has given up her neutrality, so the other teller is unlikely to engage openly
She should have started with ground rules and the purpose of the meeting before giving her own view
She should have met them separately after giving her view
Nothing; giving a preliminary view saves time
bank.explanation: A mediator's value depends on neutrality. Announcing a view at the start turns the process into a hearing with a known verdict. The other party will defend rather than explore, and any agreement will feel imposed.

bank.question: During a mediation about workload, one employee reveals that the other has repeatedly sent her unwanted messages of a sexual nature. Both had agreed that 'what is said stays in the room'. What should the manager do?
options: Keep it confidential as agreed and continue mediating the workload issue
Pause, explain this can't stay within the mediation, and route it to the harassment procedure
Ask both to add the messages to the mediation agenda, so they can resolve it together in private
Ignore it unless the employee repeats it in writing
bank.explanation: Harassment is one of the limits on mediation confidentiality and should not be mediated between the parties as an ordinary dispute. The manager should explain the limit and route it to the formal process. That is why limits are explained upfront.

bank.question: In a private caucus, Bilal tells the mediator he could live with Karachi having the Monday slot for fresh lines only, but asks her not to reveal this yet. What should the mediator do?
options: Share it with Sana straight away, since it will clearly help them reach an agreement faster today
Write it into the agreement without telling either party
Keep it private unless Bilal agrees to share it, and help him decide how to propose it himself
Tell Farhana so a decision can be imposed
bank.explanation: Caucus information is shared only with permission. Breaking that trust would end the mediator's usefulness. Coaching Bilal to make the offer himself keeps his face and his ownership of the solution.

bank.question: Which situation most clearly argues against a line manager mediating a dispute personally?
options: The dispute is between two people in different teams, so the manager has no authority over one of them
The manager has never mediated before
The dispute is about scheduling rather than relationships
One of the parties is the manager's close relative, and the other has complained about favouritism
bank.explanation: A clear conflict of interest, made worse by a favouritism complaint, means one party cannot see the mediator as neutral. Another manager or HR should mediate. Inexperience or cross-team disputes are not disqualifying on their own.

bank.question: A general manager chairs a design review with six junior engineers. He opens by giving his preferred design, then asks, 'Any concerns?' Nobody speaks, and the design later fails in testing. What change would most likely surface concerns next time?
options: Tell the engineers firmly that silence will count against them in their next annual performance appraisals
Hold the review without any engineers present
Have the engineers submit risks in writing before the meeting, and have the GM give his view last
Ask the most senior engineer to speak for everyone
bank.explanation: In hierarchical settings, a senior who speaks first anchors the room and makes disagreement feel disrespectful. Written input beforehand and the senior speaking last give face-safe channels. Threats would increase fear, not candour.

bank.question: In a family-owned textile firm, the founder's son, newly appointed director, keeps overruling the long-serving professional CEO on hiring decisions. Staff are confused and the CEO is considering resigning. What is the most durable solution?
options: Clarify decision rights through the board and a family charter, including who decides on hiring
Ask the founder to choose between them
Ask the CEO to accommodate the son, since he is family
Mediate a one-off truce between the son and the CEO, and leave the existing governance structure unchanged
bank.explanation: The conflict comes from overlapping family, ownership and management roles. Clear decision rights, agreed through governance, prevent repeated clashes. A one-off truce or forced choice leaves the structural cause in place.

bank.question: A founder-chairman rejected a digital ordering system after a junior manager criticised the current manual process as 'backward' in a board meeting. The system would genuinely help. What is the best way to reopen the idea?
options: Have the junior manager present the idea again at the next board meeting with much stronger data
Brief someone he trusts, then meet him privately with a small pilot that builds on his work
Implement the system quietly in one region without telling him
Ask all managers to sign a petition supporting the system
bank.explanation: The rejection was about lost face, not just the idea. A trusted intermediary, a private setting and framing that respects his legacy let him say yes with dignity. Going around him or using public pressure would deepen the rift.

bank.question: A contract penalty is 2% of the late consignment's value per day, capped at 10%. A consignment worth PKR 3,000,000 arrives 7 days late. The customer demands PKR 450,000. What penalty does the contract support?
bank.explanation: 7 days x 2% = 14%, but the cap is 10%. 10% of PKR 3,000,000 = PKR 300,000. PKR 420,000 ignores the cap, and PKR 450,000 is the customer's demand, not a contractual figure.

bank.question: Which of these situations should a team leader NOT try to resolve through informal mediation?
options: Two officers disagree about who should present the quarterly results
Two departments argue about the deadline for monthly reports
A manager repeatedly mocks an employee's sect in front of colleagues
A team member feels her ideas are ignored in meetings
bank.explanation: Repeated mockery of someone's religious sect is discrimination and harassment, which belongs in the formal process. The other situations are ordinary task, process or relationship conflicts suited to informal resolution.

bank.question: A night-shift packer has filed a harassment complaint against her line supervisor. While the inquiry committee investigates, what is the most appropriate interim measure?
options: Move the complainant to the day shift, on slightly lower pay, so that the two no longer meet at work
Leave both in place, since nothing has been proven
Suspend the complainant until the matter is resolved
Change supervision, for example another supervisor for her line, without disadvantaging her
bank.explanation: Interim measures should protect the complainant without penalising her, which would be retaliation. Reassigning supervision achieves that. Doing nothing leaves her exposed, and lower pay or suspension punishes the person who complained.

bank.question: A bank's RACI chart for approving loan restructuring shows: relationship manager R, credit head A, risk head A, branch manager C, operations I. Disputes keep arising over final approval. What is the best fix?
options: Add the CEO as a third Accountable person, so that there is always someone senior available to break any tie
Make one person Accountable, such as the credit head, and the risk head Consulted, with an escalation rule
Remove the branch manager from the chart
Make everyone Responsible so all share the decision
bank.explanation: Two Accountable people means two final decision-makers. Naming one A and consulting the other preserves the risk input while removing the decision clash. Adding a third A makes it worse.

bank.question: A corporate customer's admin manager posts angrily on LinkedIn that your company 'ruined our annual event' with a late catering delivery. Your contract provides a modest penalty. What is the best first response?
options: Briefly acknowledge it publicly, then call the manager privately to listen, apologise and agree a remedy
Ignore the post, as responding gives it more attention
Reply publicly with the delivery log, showing that the delay was partly caused by the customer's own changes
Ask your legal team to send a notice demanding the post be removed
bank.explanation: A brief public acknowledgement shows you care; the real conversation belongs in private, where you can listen and apply fair terms plus any goodwill gesture. Public point-scoring or legal threats escalate; silence lets the story run.

bank.question: At a pharmaceutical distributor, quality assurance and the warehouse clash every week over batch releases. QA says the warehouse ships too early; the warehouse says QA is too slow. Which package best prevents the conflict recurring?
options: Have the warehouse head report to QA
A firm memo from the CEO telling both teams to cooperate, copied to all staff in both departments
A one-off mediation between the two department heads
A turnaround agreement, a shared measure such as on-time compliant dispatch, and a daily huddle
bank.explanation: Recurring cross-department conflict needs structural fixes: clear turnaround promises, a shared measure and a regular forum. A one-off mediation or a memo can ease tensions but leaves the cause in place; changing reporting lines just moves power.

bank.question: After the Eid season, Noor Mithaas wants to make sure a gift-box failure like this year's never turns into a conflict again. Which combination addresses the structural roots most completely?
options: Annual conflict-management training for all managers, plus a rule that every dispute goes straight to the chairman
Replacing the plant manager and the regional sales manager
A shared on-time-in-full measure, one Accountable for rush orders, an order cut-off and a quarterly review
A ban on WhatsApp groups for operational matters
bank.explanation: The roots were clashing KPIs, unclear decision rights and late order changes. A shared measure, one Accountable and a cut-off agreement address each, and a review keeps them working. Training, bans or replacing people leave the structure unchanged.
